A folder the user chooses is also accepted when its `app` folder is a base directory, which is where innoextract writes a GOG installer's files, and it is a steamcmd download when it holds `steamapps/appmanifest_2310.acf`.

A file is a known file when its size in bytes and its MD5 checksum (RFC 1321) both equal one row of `FS_KNOWN_FILES`. Only a file whose size equals some row's size is hashed. Where the file sits does not change what it is.

A file that matches no row is not an error. If it loads as a PAK archive (PAK-1, PAK-2) it is reported as unrecognised, with its entry count and whether it marks the game as modified (PAK-4.2); if it cannot be opened or does not load, it is reported as unusable, with the error.

An install holds the registered game when its original base's `id1/pak1.pak` is the known registered `pak1.pak`; the shareware game when its original base has no `id1/pak1.pak` and its `id1/pak0.pak` is a known original `pak0.pak`; and the rerelease when its rerelease base's `id1/pak0.pak` is known or unrecognised, not unusable.

An install whose original base has no `id1/pak1.pak` reports `id1/pak1.pak` as missing. An install with a rerelease and no original base reports the original game's `id1/pak0.pak` and `id1/pak1.pak` as missing, since the rerelease's `id1` holds only its own `pak0.pak` (FS-5.1); this is what the Epic Games Store and Game Pass sell.

A rerelease base directory (one that holds `QuakeEX.kpf`) whose `dos` folder, matched as FS-3.7 matches names, is a base directory has that folder as the original game of the same install, with its own `id1` and game directories by FS-6.1. GOG's Quake Enhanced (product `1739637082`) installs this way: the rerelease at the top, beside `goggame-1739637082.info`, `QuakeEX.kpf`, `id1`, `hipnotic`, `rogue`, `dopa`, `mg1`, `mg3` and `ctf`, and the original DOS game in `dos`, with `dos/id1/PAK0.PAK` of 18,689,235 bytes and `dos/id1/PAK1.PAK` of 34,257,856 bytes (the 1.06 `pak0.pak` and the registered `pak1.pak` of `FS_KNOWN_FILES`), `dos/hipnotic/pak0.pak` and `dos/rogue/pak0.pak`. No published source gives this layout; it was read from Justin's GOG install on 2026-10-16, [#277](https://github.com/quakecstudio/editor/issues/277#issuecomment-6221264809).

A code is `E` (error) or `W` (warning) and four digits. The first two digits are the group: `01` lexical, `02` declarations and types, `03` expressions and statements, `04` project, limits and fatal errors, `05` errors this compiler adds where id's `qcc` has undefined behaviour (QC-27). Warnings use the same groups.
A code is never reused for a different diagnostic. A diagnostic that no longer applies is withdrawn with its statement, and its code stays unassigned.

Every diagnostic has a primary span: the token the rule names, or, for errors id's `qcc` raises at its lookahead token, the construct the rule is about. id's own report is `<file>:<line>:<message>` with the line of QC-1.5; the vanilla profile's differential tests compare messages and codes, not lines.

For the errors id's `qcc` raises, the message is id's text, with `%s` and `%i` filled in as id does. The parser keeps going after an error with recovery of its own (LANG-2); the error limit and stop-at-first-file of QC-24 are id's behaviour, not requirements on this compiler.

A source file is a sequence of bytes with no encoding. The text ends at the first NUL byte; anything after it is ignored.
Line numbers start at 1 and increase by one at each LF (0x0A) byte. CR (0x0D) is whitespace and never starts a line, so CRLF and LF files have the same line numbers.
Bytes 0x80 to 0xFF outside a string literal are whitespace. `PR_LexWhitespace` skips every byte whose `char` value is `<= ' '`, and `char` is signed on the x86 build, so these bytes are negative.
Bytes 0x80 to 0xFF inside a string literal are copied into the string unchanged.

The line number recorded for an emitted statement is the line of the token the lexer holds when the statement is emitted: the token after the last one the statement consumed. In `if (a)` followed by `{` on the next line, the `IFNOT` gets the line of `{`.
Whitespace is every byte from 0x01 to 0x20, plus the bytes in QC-1.3. It separates tokens and is otherwise ignored.

`//` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. A `//` comment with no LF after it ends the file. (id's loop then steps past the terminating NUL and reads beyond the buffer; the reference build ends the file there, and this spec fixes that answer.)
`/*` starts a comment that ends at the first `*/` found by a scan that starts at the `*` of the `/*`. So `/*/` is a complete comment, and comments do not nest.
A `/*` comment with no closing `*/` stops one byte before the end of the file, and that last byte is then lexed as a token. QC-27.2 replaces this with an error.
Line breaks inside a comment count towards line numbers (QC-1.2).
A comment may stand between any two tokens, and between the components of a vector literal (QC-5.3). Inside a string literal, `//` and `/*` are text.
A name starts with an ASCII letter or `_` and continues with ASCII letters, digits and `_`. Case matters.

No name is reserved. The words `float`, `vector`, `string`, `entity`, `void`, `local`, `return`, `if`, `else`, `while` and `do` act as keywords only where the parser compares the current token with them: types at the start of a declaration or parameter, statement keywords at the start of a statement, `else` after an `if` statement and `while` after a `do` body. Anywhere else they are ordinary names, so `float do;` declares a global `do` and `a = do;` reads it, but a statement `do = 1;` starts a `do` loop.
A name of 63 bytes or more is an error, "name too long" (`PR_ParseName` tests `strlen(pr_token) >= MAX_NAME-1`). 62 bytes is accepted. LIMIT-7.2 states the same limit.

`PR_Check` and `PR_Expect` compare the text of the current token whatever its kind, and a string literal's text is its contents. So a string literal whose contents are a keyword or punctuation is taken as that keyword or punctuation wherever the parser checks for one: `"if" (a) b = 1;` compiles as an `if` statement. QC-27.3 diverges.
`for`, `break`, `continue`, `switch`, `case`, `goto`, `int`, `const` and every other word not in QC-3.2 have no meaning to vanilla `qcc`; they are names.
A float literal starts with a digit, or with `-` immediately followed by a digit, and continues over digits and `.` characters. Its value is C `atof` of that text, rounded to a 32-bit float.

A `-` immediately followed by a digit is always the start of a negative literal, whatever precedes it. `a-5` is the name `a` then the literal `-5`, which is an error ("expected ;, found -5" in a statement); `a - 5` and `a - -5` subtract.
`atof` stops at the second `.`, so `1.2.3` is one token whose value is 1.2.
There are no exponents, hex or suffixes: `1e5` is the literal `1` then the name `e5`. A literal cannot start with `.`: `.5` is the `.` operator then `5`.
There is no unary minus operator. `-` before anything but a digit is binary subtraction, so `a = -b;` is an error, "not a name"; id 1.01 writes `0 - b`.
A vector literal is `'`, three numbers, `'`. Each number is read as in QC-4.1, except that its first byte is taken whatever it is, so each component may be negative.
After each component the lexer skips whitespace and comments. If the byte after the third component is not `'`, it is an error, "Bad vector".
Whitespace (including line breaks) and comments may appear between the components and before the closing quote, and count towards line numbers.
A string literal is `"`, its contents, `"`. There is no concatenation of adjacent literals.
`\n` in the contents is one LF byte and `\"` is one `"` byte. A backslash followed by anything else, including a second backslash, is an error, "Unknown escape char".
A line break inside the literal is an error, "newline inside quote"; the end of the file inside it, or after its backslash, is an error, "EOF inside quote".
The contents are at most `QC_MAX_TOKEN - 1` bytes. id's lexer does not check and overruns `pr_token`; QC-27.4 makes a longer literal an error.

The punctuation tokens are, in the order the lexer tries them: `&&` `||` `<=` `>=` `==` `!=` `;` `,` `!` `*` `/` `(` `)` `-` `+` `=` `[` `]` `{` `}` `...` `.` `<` `>` `#` `&` `|`. The first one that matches the input wins, which is the longest match for every prefix pair in the list.

Any other byte that does not start a token (for example `%`, `^`, `~`, `?`, `:`, `@`, `\` or a backquote) is an error, "Unknown punctuation". The lexer does not advance past it, so recovery (QC-24.3) meets it again until the error limit stops the file.
`{` and `}` also adjust a brace depth that error recovery uses (QC-24.3).
There are no compound assignment, increment or decrement operators, no `%`, `^`, `~`, `?:`, shifts or comma operator. `qcc.h`: "There are no ++ / -- operators, or operate/assign operators."

`$` followed by a word starts a `$` command or a frame macro reference. The word runs from the first byte after `$` and any blanks to the next byte that is whitespace, `,` or `;`. `$` followed only by blanks before the end of the line is an error, "hanging $".

`$frame` defines frame macros: each word after it on the same line, split at whitespace, is appended to the file's frame list. The first frame defined in a file is 0, the next 1, and so on, across all `$frame` lines in the file.
The frame list is cleared at the start of each source file, so a frame macro is visible only in the file that defines it, after its `$frame` line.
`$cd`, `$origin`, `$base`, `$flags`, `$scale` and `$skin` are ignored with the rest of their line.

Any other `$word` is a frame macro reference. It becomes a float literal whose value is the index of the first frame in the list whose name equals the word; it can stand wherever a float literal can, including a global initialiser and a state function's frame (QC-13.6). A word not in the list is an error, "Unknown frame macro $word".
Because the word ends only at whitespace, `,` or `;`, a reference followed directly by another character includes it: `($b)` looks up `b)` and fails.
A frame name defined twice keeps its first index; the second definition still takes the next index, which no reference can reach.

`$modelname`, `$framegroupstart`, `$framegroupend`, `$load`, `$spritename` and `$type` (modelgen and spritegen commands that id 1.01's `models.qc` and `sprites.qc` use) are not `qcc` commands: they are references to undefined frame macros and fail as in QC-8.5. Those two files are not in id 1.01's `progs.src`. `$modelname` as FTEQCC reads it is part of the FTEQCC dialect spec (P2-01).

A `,` or `;` on a `$frame` line makes id's `qcc` loop forever appending empty names past the end of the frame table, and a frame name of 16 bytes or more overruns its slot into the next. QC-27.5 and QC-27.6 define what this compiler does.

A directive is a line, outside any comment, whose first non-blank byte is `#` followed, after optional blanks, by a name. A `#` anywhere else, or followed by anything but a name, is the `#` token. No program id's `qcc` accepts has a line that starts with `#` and a name, because a vanilla `#` is always followed by a number (QC-13.3), so the preprocessor changes nothing for vanilla code.

`#include "path"` replaces the directive with the contents of the named file, resolved relative to the directory of the file containing the directive, or, when no file is there, as QC-9.20 says. Diagnostics and statements in the included text carry the included file's name and lines.

`#define NAME` and `#define NAME text` define an object-like macro whose body is the rest of the line, trimmed. `#define NAME(a, b) text`, with the `(` directly after the name, defines a function-like macro. A later identical `#define` of the same name is accepted; a different one replaces the old one with a warning.

After its definition, a name token that matches a macro is replaced by its body, and a function-like macro's parameters in the body are replaced by the comma-separated arguments of the use. The replacement is rescanned for further macros, except the macro being expanded. Names inside string literals and comments are never replaced.
`#undef NAME` removes a macro; removing one that is not defined does nothing.

`#ifdef NAME` and `#ifndef NAME` start a conditional block that is kept when the name is (or is not) a defined macro. `#else` flips it and `#endif` closes it. Blocks nest; directives inside a skipped block are only counted for nesting. A `#else` or `#endif` without an open block, or a block still open at the end of the file, is an error.
Every token produced by expansion keeps the span of the macro use it came from, and the span of its text in the macro definition, so a diagnostic can point at both (LANG-1).
Macros and conditional state run on across the files of one `progs.src`, in compilation order (QC-23.3); frame macros do not (QC-8.3).

A directive name other than `include`, `define`, `undef`, `ifdef`, `ifndef`, `else` and `endif` is an error outside a skipped block, and so is a directive whose operand is missing or malformed: `#include` without a string literal, `#define`, `#undef`, `#ifdef` or `#ifndef` without a name, or a parameter list that is not names separated by `,` and closed by `)`. The directive line is then dropped. Tokens after the operand of `#include`, `#undef`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#else` and `#endif` are ignored.

A function-like macro name not followed by `(` is an ordinary name and is not replaced. A use whose argument count differs from the parameter count, or whose argument list is not closed by `)` before the end of the file, is an error; the use is left unreplaced. Arguments are split at commas outside parentheses, and `F()` passes no arguments.
An `#include` of a file that cannot be read, or of a file that is already being included (directly or through other includes), is an error, and the directive is dropped.

A conditional block is closed in the file that opens it, whether that file is listed in `progs.src` or included. At the end of each file, every block it opened that is still open is reported (QC-9.6) and closed, so the next file starts outside it.
**Withdrawn** (P2-78, #484): it said the FTEQCC profile keeps QC-9.4's rule against self-expansion. Replaced by QC-9.17 and `dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.17 and FTEF-14.19.
**Withdrawn** (P2-77, #482): it said an argument written against a body token stays apart from it under FTEQCC too. Replaced by QC-9.15.
**Withdrawn** (P2-78, #484): it said a token the preprocessor made touches nothing. Replaced by QC-9.16.

An expansion keeps the spacing of the text it came from: two tokens that touch in a macro's body, or in one argument of it, touch in the expansion, and two that do not, or that come from different macros or a macro and the text around its use, are apart. A rule that reads whether two tokens touch then reads a macro's tokens as it reads the source: under FTEQCC `#define B #5` then `void() f = B;` is the builtin 5 (FTE-23.1), and `#define L lbl:` used as a statement is a label (FTEF-18.23). Under FTEQCC a token a `##` paste or a `#` string made is written into the expansion as text (FTEF-14.14, FTEF-14.31), and touches as that text stands: with `#define P(a,b) a##b:`, `P(l,bl)` is the label `lbl:`; a built-in constant's value is a chunk of its own and touches nothing (FTEF-14.17). In the vanilla dialect an argument's tokens are apart from the body's. FTEQCC reads an expansion as text (`qcc_pr_lex.c`, fte-team/fteqw@`f937b9d88f71fc4429db5fe56c6a98d922711b2e`): `QCC_PR_IncludeChunkEx` lexes the body as `QCC_PR_PreProcessor_Define` stored it, which drops each `/* */` comment ("multi-line c style comments become part of the define itself", skipped to the `*/` and not copied) and each `\` before a line break, so tokens with only those between them touch under FTEQCC: `#define L lbl/**/:` is a label. `QCC_PR_ExpandPreProcessorMacro` substitutes an argument into the body as text: it copies the body's white space (`QCC_PR_LexWhitespace(true)` then `QCC_PR_ExpandStrCat`) and, for a parameter, the argument's tokens each with what stands before it, white space and comments before its first token dropped (`QCC_PR_LexWhitespace(false)` after the `(` and each `,`) and white space and `//` comments after its last too (the copy loop stops when `QCC_COM_Parse2`, which skips those but not a `/* */` comment, finds no token), and the variadic argument whole, anything before its `)` kept (`QCC_PR_ExpandStrCat(..., paramoffset[c->numparams], strlen(...))`). So under FTEQCC an argument's first token touches the body token before the parameter when the parameter touches it, an argument's last token touches the body token after the parameter when the parameter touches that and nothing the copy keeps follows the argument, and an empty argument leaves the body tokens either side touching when both touch the parameter: `#define L(x) x:` used as `L(lbl)`, `L( lbl)` or `L(lbl )` is the label `lbl:` and as `L(lbl/**/)` is not, `#define V(...) __VA_ARGS__:` used as `V(lbl)` is a label and as `V(lbl )` is not, `#define L(x,y) x y:` used as `L(,lbl)` is a label and as `L(lbl,)` is not, and the pinned FTEQCC compiles each so. A token touches only the one written right before it, so tokens that an expansion to nothing came to stand between stay apart: with `#define E`, `#define K lbl E:` used as a statement is no label, as FTEQCC reads `lbl`, then `E` and the `:` after a space. A parameter that under FTEQCC touches a word across what `QCC_PR_PreProcessor_Define` drops is part of that word as stored, which `QCC_COM_Parse2` reads as one token, and no parameter: `#define A(a) a/**/b` is the name `ab` (the pinned FTEQCC: "Unknown value \"ab\""), while a number before a parameter ends at it.

Expansion nests to any depth, with no limit on the depth and no diagnostic for it: a chain of macros, each defined as the name of the one before (`#define M1 M0`, `#define M2 M1`, ...), is rescanned to its end however long it is, and no chain exhausts the stack. FTEQCC sets no nesting limit: `QCC_PR_CheckCompConst` (`qcc_pr_lex.c`, fte-team/fteqw@`f937b9d88f71fc4429db5fe56c6a98d922711b2e`) expands a macro unless `currentchunk->cnst != c` fails (`//macros don't expand themselves`) or, for an object-like macro, `if (c->inside >= 8)`, which counts only that macro's own open expansions; each expansion is pushed by `QCC_PR_IncludeChunkEx` as a heap-allocated chunk (`qcc_includechunk_t *chunk = qccHunkAlloc(sizeof(qcc_includechunk_t)); chunk->prev = currentchunk;`), not a C stack frame. But `QCC_PR_Lex` calls itself once for each expansion (`//we expanded a macro. we need to read the tokens out of it now though`, then `QCC_PR_Lex();`), so a long enough chain exhausts FTEQCC's own stack: the pinned FTEQCC, built by `cargo xtask oracles build` on macOS arm64 with its 8 MiB main stack, compiles `float x = M49999;` after a 50000-long chain to `x = 1` and dies with `SIGSEGV` at 100000. Expanding every chain to its end is a deliberate divergence from that crash, which depends on the host's stack, not on the program. id's `qcc` has no macros (QC-9). In the vanilla dialect the rule against self-expansion is QC-9.4's; under FTEQCC it is FTEQCC's (`dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.17), with this profile's bound on the work (FTEF-14.28).

The preprocessor makes at most `FTE_MAX_EXPANSIONS` = 2^20 macro expansions in one file and writes at most `FTE_MAX_EXPANDED_TOKENS` = 2^22 tokens with them, under the vanilla dialect as under FTEQCC (`dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.28), an expansion's tokens counted before it is written, each body token one and each parameter its argument's: a function-like macro whose body names its parameter `n` times writes its argument `n` times, so one expansion alone could write the square of its file's length (a 32018-byte file of `#define D(x)`, 8000 `x` and `D(` given 8000 tokens, 64000000 tokens). The first use past either bound is "macro expansion too large" (`E0120`, QCD-8.13), reported once, and it and later uses are left as written. id's `qcc` has no macros (QC-9), so the bound is this project's own, that no file exhausts the memory of the semantic model, which preprocesses on every edit.

The semantic model parses the preprocessor's output as text with no directive lines (`qc_syntax::parse_preprocessed`): every directive has run, so a `#` left in the output is the `#` token in both dialects, first on its line too, as one after a `/* */` comment at a line's start (QC-9.1) or one a macro's body writes. id's `qcc`, which has no preprocessor, reads such a `#` as any other: `/* c */#foo` at the top level is `"#" is not a type` (`E0203`), `void() f =` before `/* c */#foo;` on the next line is "Bad builtin immediate" (`E0209`), and `void() f =` before `/* c */#5;` is builtin 5. The vanilla profile reports the same. Under FTEQCC, whose preprocessor leaves `#foo` when `foo` names no macro (`dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.52), the pinned FTEQCC refuses the first two ("Explicit precompiler usage when not defined foo") and takes the third, and so does the profile, with the parser's errors. The tree of a file as written keeps its directive lines (QC-9.1).

An `#include` whose path names no readable file beside the file containing it is looked for in the module's include directories (`include_dirs`, PRJ-5.2), in order, as the project graph finds it, and the first that names a readable file is read; a path that is not relative is looked for only where it names. When none is readable it is QC-9.11's error, which names the path beside the including file. So a module whose `quakec.toml` gives `include_dirs = ["lib"]` reads `lib/inc.qh` for `#include "inc.qh"` in `src/main.qc`, and `src/inc.qh` when that exists. id's `qcc` has no `#include` (QC-9), and FTEQCC's own search is `dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.40 and FTEF-14.49.
The simple types are `void`, `float`, `vector`, `string` and `entity`. A `vector` is three floats; every other type is one 32-bit word.
`.T` is the type of a field holding a `T`, for any type `T`, including a function type and another field type (`..float` is accepted).

`T(T1 n1, T2 n2, ...)` is the type of a function returning the simple type `T` with those parameters; `T()` takes none. A parameter's type may itself be a field or function type. The parameter names are part of the declaration, not the type (QC-13.11).
`T(...)` is a function taking any number of arguments of any types. `...` must be the whole parameter list: `void(float a, ...)` is an error, `"..." is not a type`.
A function type cannot return a function: after `T(...)` the type ends, so `void()()` is not a type.

**Withdrawn** (P2-136, #587): it said two function types with the same return type, parameter count and parameter types are one type, but `PR_FindType` never finds a variadic type again. Replaced by QC-10.10.
A variable of type `void` may be declared; it occupies one word.
A function type with more than eight parameters is accepted by id's `qcc`, which writes past `parm_types[8]`; QC-27.7 makes it an error.
There is no `int`, array, struct, pointer or `const` type in the source language. The compiler uses a pointer type internally for field stores (QC-17.3).

Two function or field types are the same type when they have the same return or field type, the same parameter count and the same parameter types; parameter names do not matter (`PR_FindType` interns them). A variadic function type, `num_parms` -1, is never found again: `PR_FindType`'s loop `for (i=0 ; i< type->num_parms ; i++)` ends at once, and `if (i == type->num_parms)` is then false, so each `T(...)` written is a type of its own and a function type holding one is too. So `void(...) va; void(...) va;` is "Type mismatch on redeclaration of va", and an argument of such a type matches no parameter.

A file is a sequence of declarations: a type, then one or more names separated by `,`, each optionally followed by `=` and an initialiser, then `;`. At file level there is nothing else: no statements and no stray `;`.

A declaration of a function type with an initialiser defines the function (QC-13). A function definition in a list is followed by `,` or `;` like any other name, so `void() a = {}, b = {};` defines two functions, and the `;` after a function body is required. `qcc.h`: "Don't forget the ; after the trailing brace of a function initialization."

Any other initialiser must be a single literal (or frame macro reference) whose type is exactly the declared type: a float, vector or string literal for `float`, `vector` or `string`. No initialiser is valid for `entity`, `void` or a field type; those are errors, "wrong immediate type for NAME".

id's `qcc` checks the initialiser's type against the type of the last literal the lexer read, without checking that the current token is a literal. So `float x = y;` after any earlier float literal is accepted and initialises `x` with that earlier literal's value, and the name `y` is consumed. QC-27.8 makes a non-literal initialiser an error.

An initialised declaration marks the definition initialised. A declaration of a name that already exists in scope with the same type refers to the same definition, so a name may be declared any number of times and initialised once. Declaring it with a different type is an error, "Type mismatch on redeclaration of NAME"; initialising it a second time is an error, "NAME redeclared".

An initialised global is a constant: its value is stored in the global area of the progs, it is not saved in saved games (QC-21.6), and literals of the same value reuse it (QC-20.2). Nothing stops code from assigning to it. `qcc.h`: "Anything that is initialized is assumed to be constant, and will have immediates folded into it. If you change the value, your program will malfunction."

Declaring a `vector` named `v` also declares `float` definitions `v_x`, `v_y` and `v_z` at its three words; declaring a field `.vector f` also declares `.float` fields `f_x`, `f_y` and `f_z` at its three field offsets. These are ordinary names (QC-15.7).

Every global function must be defined somewhere in the program; at the end of compilation each one that is not is reported, "function NAME was not defined", and compilation fails. A global of function type is therefore always a function, never a variable.
Fields and functions can only be declared at file level: `local .float f;` and `local void() g;` are errors, "Fields and functions must be global". Parameters of function type are allowed.

`local` declarations inside a function body have the same grammar as QC-11.1 and QC-11.3. A local initialiser is stored once in the progs' global area, like a global constant; it is not executed on each call, and later literals of the same value reuse the local (QC-20.2).

A vector's initialiser does not initialise its components: `PR_ParseDefs` sets `def->initialized = 1;` on the vector's definition only, and `PR_GetDef` made the components as definitions of their own. So `vector v = '1 2 3'; float v_x = 2;` compiles, and writes 2 over the vector's first word.

A `.vector` field's components are made with `qcc`'s own `type_floatfield` (`PR_GetDef (&type_floatfield, element, scope, true);`), a type `PR_FindType` never returns, since `pr.types` holds only `type_function` and the types it interned (`InitData`: `pr.types = &type_function;`). So a component and a `.float` written in the source are of different types, in either order: `.vector fv; .float fv_x;` and `.float fv_x; .vector fv;` are "Type mismatch on redeclaration of fv_x". A `float` or a `void()` is the same type however made: `type_float` and `type_function` are the ones the parser gives.

A local's initialiser initialises the definition the local is, and that definition may be initialised once (QC-11.5): `local float y = 1; local float y = 2;` is "y redeclared", and so is a local initialised where its name is an initialised global, or a global an earlier function's local initialised (QC-12.3).
There are two scopes: global, and the function being defined. Blocks do not open scopes; a `local` anywhere in a function body is visible from its declaration to the end of the function.

All definitions, global and local, are kept in one list in declaration order. A name is looked up by walking that list from the start and taking the first definition with that name that is global or belongs to the current function.

A local or parameter cannot shadow a global declared before it: the lookup in `local float x;` or in the parameter `x` finds the global `x` first and reuses it (or reports a type mismatch if the types differ). Both then read and write the global.

A local of one function is invisible to every other function, so two functions may declare locals with the same name, and a global declared later may take a name that an earlier function used for a local.

Names are resolved when they are parsed: a function body sees only the definitions made before it in compilation order (QC-23.3). Using a name before any declaration is an error, "Unknown value \"NAME\"". `qcc.h`: "Source files are processed sequentially without dumping any state, so if a defs file is the first one processed, the definitions will be available to all other files."
The next-think name in a state function header is declared on the spot as a global `void()` when it does not exist yet (QC-13.6).
A function is defined by `= body`, `= [frame, next] body` or `= #number` on a declaration of function type. A body is `{`, zero or more statements, `}`; an empty body is allowed.

**Withdrawn** (P2-120, #612): it said the body's parameter names are the ones written in the defining declaration's type, but a parameter of function type with parameters writes over them. Replaced by QC-13.11.

`#n` makes the function the engine builtin number `n`: the function record's `first_statement` is `-n` and no statements are emitted. `n` must be a float literal with an integral value, else "Bad builtin immediate"; `#1.5` is rejected. Builtins allocate no parameter or local storage.

`#0` and negative numbers are accepted. `#0` leaves `first_statement` uninitialised in id's `qcc` (the reference build wrote 0), and `#-1` writes `first_statement` 1, a call to statement 1. QC-27.9 makes both errors.

Parameters are allocated first, in order, at consecutive global offsets; then the body's locals and temporaries as they are met (QC-21.4). If a parameter resolves to a global (QC-12.3) at a lower offset than the previous parameter, `qcc` stops with the fatal error "bad parm order".

In `= [frame, next] body`, `frame` must be a float literal or frame macro reference, else "state frame must be a number", and `next` a name, which is declared as a global `void()` if it does not exist and must have that type if it does ("Type mismatch on redeclaration of NAME"). The first statement of the function is then `STATE frame, next`. When it runs, the engine sets `self.nextthink` to `time + 0.1`, `self.frame` to `frame` and `self.think` to `next` (`OP_STATE` in `pr_exec.c`).
A body ends with a `DONE` statement after its last statement, so falling off the end returns.
Neither the return type nor the presence of a return value is checked: `return "x";` in a `float()` and `return;` in a `float()` both compile (`qcc.h` lists "return type checking" under TODO).

A function record holds `first_statement`, `parm_start` (the offset of its first parameter), `locals` (QC-21.4), the name and file as string offsets, `numparms` and each parameter's size in words. A variadic function's `numparms` is -1.

The builtin number is the literal's 32-bit float value (QC-4.1) converted to `int`, so above 2^24 it is the float's, not the digits': `PR_ParseImmediateStatements` (`qcc/pr_comp.c`, id-Software/Quake-Tools@`c0d1b91c74eb654365ac7755bc837e497caaca73`) reads `if (pr_token_type != tt_immediate || pr_immediate_type != &type_float || pr_immediate._float != (int)pr_immediate._float) PR_ParseError ("Bad builtin immediate"); f->builtin = (int)pr_immediate._float;`, where `PR_LexNumber` gives `return atof (pr_token);`. `#16777217` is builtin 16777216 and `#123456789` is 123456792. A value outside -2^31 to 2^31 - 1 is "Bad builtin immediate": C leaves its conversion to `int` undefined, and the x86 build gives -2147483648 (VM-9.2), which differs from the value. id's `qcc` built for arm64 by `cargo xtask oracles build` saturates instead and binds `#2147483648` as 2147483647; the x86 result is the rule.

The parameter names used inside the body come from the defining declaration's type, as `pr_parm_names` holds them once that type is read; names in prototypes are ignored (`qcc.h`: "The names are ignored except when the function is initialized."). `PR_ParseType` (`qcc/pr_lex.c`, id-Software/Quake-Tools@`c0d1b91c74eb654365ac7755bc837e497caaca73`) reads each parameter as `type = PR_ParseType (); name = PR_ParseName (); strcpy (pr_parm_names[new.num_parms], name);`, and `PR_ParseImmediateStatements` (`qcc/pr_comp.c`) defines parameter `i` as `PR_GetDef (type->parm_types[i], pr_parm_names[i], pr_scope, true)`. So a parameter whose type is a function type with parameters, or a field of one, first writes those parameters' names from index 0, and the parameter's own name is written after. In `void(float b, void(float q) cb) f` the body's parameters are `q` and `cb`: `b` is `Unknown value "b"`. FTEQCC keeps each parameter's own name: its `QCC_PR_ParseFunctionType` (`engine/qclib/qcc_pr_lex.c`, fte-team/fteqw@`f937b9d88f71fc4429db5fe56c6a98d922711b2e`) writes `pr_parm_names` only when `int definenames = !recursivefunctiontype;`, the outermost function type.
A statement is a block, `return`, `while`, `do`, `local`, `if` or an expression followed by `;`, chosen by the first token (QC-3.2).
A block `{ ... }` inside a function holds one or more statements. `{}` inside a body is an error ("not a name"), as is a lone `;`: there is no empty statement.
`return;` emits `RETURN` with no operand; `return e;` emits `RETURN e`.
`if (e) s` emits `IFNOT e, +n` jumping past `s`. `if (e) s1 else s2` emits `IFNOT e` jumping to `s2`, and a `GOTO` after `s1` jumping past `s2`. `else` binds to the nearest `if`.
`while (e) s` emits the condition, `IFNOT` past the loop, `s`, then a `GOTO` back to the first statement of the condition.
`do s while (e);` emits `s`, the condition, then `IF e` back to the first statement of `s`. The `;` is required.
The parentheses around an `if`, `while` or `do` condition are required.
There is no `for`, `switch`, `break`, `continue` or `goto`.
An expression statement may be any expression; one with no effect, such as `a;`, is accepted and its statements are emitted.
Binary operators have the priorities and associativity in the table below, tightest first.
`&` and `|` bind as tightly as `*` and `/`, so `b & c | 4` is `(b & c) | 4` and `a + b & c` is `a + (b & c)`.
`=` binds tighter than `&&` and `||`: `a = b && c` is `(a = b) && c`, and `a && b = c` is `a && (b = c)`.
`&&` and `||` have the same priority and associate left: `a || b && c` is `(a || b) && c`.
Comparisons associate left: `a == b == c` is `(a == b) == c`.
`!` is the only prefix operator. Its operand is an expression at priority 4, so `!a == b` is `!(a == b)` and `!a + b` is `!(a + b)`, while `!a && b` is `(!a) && b`.
A term is `!` expression, `(` expression `)`, a literal, a frame macro reference or a name. `v_x`, `v_y` and `v_z` are names (QC-11.7), not an operator.

The left operand of a call is the term or field access before `(`. A call ends the priority-1 loop, so neither `g().fl` nor `g()()` parses: `expected ;, found .`. Field access chains: `e.en.hp` is `(e.en).hp`.
Operands are evaluated left to right, and each operator's statement is emitted after both operands' statements; every operator result goes into a new temporary (QC-21.5).
`&&` and `||` evaluate both operands. `qcc.h`: "The && and || operators DO NOT EARLY OUT like C!"
The binary operators accept exactly the operand types in the table below and give its result types, emitting the named opcode.

There is no `vector / float`, no ordering of vectors, strings or entities, no equality of fields, and no `&&`, `||`, `&` or `|` on anything but floats: `if (e && a)` with an entity `e` is an error, "type mismatch for &&".

**Withdrawn** (P2-136, #587): it said two function operands of `==` must have the same function type, but `PR_Expression` compares only the basic types (`type_a != op->type_a->type->type`), so `f1 == g` of two function types is taken. Replaced by QC-16.7.
`!` accepts float, vector, string, entity and function operands and emits `NOT_F`, `NOT_V`, `NOT_S`, `NOT_ENT` or `NOT_FNC`; a field operand is an error, "type mismatch for !". The result is a float.

What the engine computes: `&` and `|` convert both floats to `int`, combine them and convert back (`OP_BITAND`, `OP_BITOR`); `&&` and `||` treat a float as true when it is not 0.0 (`OP_AND`, `OP_OR`); `NOT_V` is true when all three components are 0.0; `NOT_S` is true for the null string and for an empty string; `NOT_ENT` is true for the world entity; `EQ_S` compares string contents. The VM spec states the full rules.
A field access `e.f` reads the field `f` of entity `e`. On the left of `=` it becomes a store into the field (QC-17.3).
**Withdrawn** (#84): it said `.` refuses a field of `void`; the field's `type_c` of `ev_void` is not compared, and QC-16.8 replaces it.

A row matches by the operands' basic types alone (`type_a != op->type_a->type->type || type_b != ...`): two functions of any types are `EQ_FNC`'s, and an assignment's target and value must be of one basic type among float, vector, string, entity, field and function (`STORE_*`, and `STOREP_*` for a field of an entity, whose value must be of the field's type); any other is "type mismatch for =". `.` takes an entity and a field, its row the one whose result is the field's type; a `.void` field's `type_c` is `ev_void`, which the loop does not compare (`type_c != ev_void && ...`), so the first row is taken and the value is a float: `x = e.fv;` of a `.void fv` is no error. Anything else is "type mismatch for .". Each mismatch is `PR_ParseError`, which ends the statement. Source: id-Software/Quake-Tools@c0d1b91c74eb654365ac7755bc837e497caaca73, `qcc/pr_comp.c`, `PR_Expression`.

**Withdrawn** (P2-06, #62): it said `x = e` requires `x` and `e` to have the same type, but the store's row is chosen by basic types (QC-16.8), so two fields or two functions of different types are assigned. Replaced by QC-17.6.

id's `qcc` does not check that the left side can be assigned: `5 = a;` stores into the literal's global, `f() = 3` into the return slot and `(a + b) = 3` into a temporary. QC-27.10 makes these errors.

When `=` is met and the last statement emitted so far is a `LOAD_*`, that statement is rewritten to `ADDRESS` (its result becomes a pointer to the field) and the assignment emits `STOREP_F`, `STOREP_V`, `STOREP_S`, `STOREP_ENT`, `STOREP_FLD` or `STOREP_FNC`, storing the right side through the pointer. This is how `e.f = x` stores into a field; in `e.en.hp = 3` only the last access becomes `ADDRESS`.

QC-17.3 looks at the last statement emitted, not at the left operand. If the previous statement ended with a field load and the next assignment's left side is a plain name, the earlier load is rewritten and the name's definition is retyped as a pointer: `e.fl; a = 2;` emits `ADDRESS e, fl, t` and `STOREP_F 2, a`. QC-27.11 diverges.
There are no compound assignments (QC-7.4).

`x = e` requires `x` and `e` to have the same basic type (QC-16.8) and emits `STORE_F`, `STORE_V`, `STORE_S`, `STORE_ENT`, `STORE_FLD` or `STORE_FNC` by it, with `e` as operand a and `x` as operand b: `fa = fb;` with `.float fa` and `.vector fb` is `STORE_FLD fb, fa`. Its value is `e`, so `a = b = c` stores `c` into `b` and then `c` into `a`.

Through a field (QC-17.3) the value must have the basic type of what the field holds: `PR_Expression` checks `if (type_a == ev_pointer && type_b != e->type->aux_type->type)`, so `e.fv = 1` with `.vector fv` is "type mismatch for =". The address keeps the temporary its load had, three words for a vector field (QC-21.5).

**Withdrawn** (P2-136, #587): it said fewer arguments than a fixed parameter list is "too few parameters", but `PR_ParseFunctionCall` checks the count only when the call has an argument (`if (!PR_Check(")")) { ... }`), so `f1()` of a `void(float x) f1` is taken. Replaced by QC-18.8.
A variadic function (QC-10.4) takes up to eight arguments of any types; nine or more is an error, "More than eight parameters".

Each argument is evaluated and immediately copied to its parameter slot with `STORE_V` (three words, whatever its type), slot `i` being global offset `4 + 3i`. After the last argument, `CALLn f` is emitted, `n` the argument count.
The call's value is the global at offset 1 (`OFS_RETURN`), typed as the function's return type.

Because the slots are shared, a call inside a later argument overwrites the slots of earlier arguments: in `g(4, h(1))`, `h`'s argument is stored into slot 0 over the 4, so `g` receives 1. `qcc.h`: "afunc ( 4, bfunc(1,2,3)); will fail because there is a shared parameter marshaling area, which will cause the 1 from bfunc to overwrite the 4 allready placed in parm0."

Because the return slot is shared, two calls in one expression read the same slot after both calls: `g() + h()` adds `h()`'s result to itself. `qcc.h`: "total = factorial(3) + factorial(4); Will fail because the return value from functions is held in a single global area."
A call through a field, `e.th()`, loads the function from the field and calls the loaded value.

`f(a1, ..., an)` requires `f` to have a function type, else "not a function". With at least one argument and a fixed parameter list, an argument past the last parameter is an error, "too many parameters" (raised before it is parsed), an argument whose type is not exactly the parameter's is "type mismatch on parm N", counting from 0, and fewer arguments than parameters "too few parameters"; a call with none is checked for no count. Each is `PR_ParseError`, which ends the statement.

The return value's global has the type of the last call made when an operator reads its operands' types, after both are parsed: `qcc` keeps one `def_ret` and retypes it at each call (`def_ret.type = t->aux_type;`). With `float() g` and `vector() h`, `g() + h()` adds two vectors, `ADD_V`, and `h() * g()` multiplies two floats, `MUL_F`.

There are no implicit conversions and no casts. Every operand, argument and assigned value must have exactly the required type; the only exceptions are QC-19.2, QC-19.3 and the variadic arguments of QC-18.2.

The condition of `if`, `while` and `do` may have any type. The statement tests the first word of the value as a 32-bit integer (`if (!a->_int)` in `OP_IFNOT`): a float is false only when it is +0.0 (-0.0 is true), a string only when it is the null string, an entity only when it is the world, a function only when it is null.
A vector condition tests only its first word, the x component: `if (v)` emits `IFNOT v_x`, so `'0 0 1'` is false. `!v` tests all three (QC-16.5).
An empty string literal is not the null string: `if ("")` is true and `!""` is true (QC-16.5).
A `return` value is not converted or checked (QC-13.8); the engine copies three words from it into the return slot (`OP_RETURN`).
Every literal in an expression is a global holding its value. A string literal's text is copied into the string table and the global holds its offset.

Before allocating one, `qcc` walks all definitions in order and reuses the first initialised definition of the same type and equal value: a named constant, a local initialiser, or an earlier literal. Floats compare with `==`, vectors component by component with `==`, strings by the text at the definition's string offset.
Since `0.0 == -0.0`, `0` and `-0` share one global, holding whichever was met first.
A new literal's definition is named `IMMEDIATE`, is global, and is written to the global definitions table like any other definition (QC-25.3).
A string literal's text is copied into the string table once, when its global is allocated; a reused literal adds nothing.

A `string` declaration initialiser does not copy its text anywhere. The global receives the first word of the lexer's last literal value: the string offset of the last string literal allocated by QC-20.1, or the bits of the last float or vector literal read, whichever came last, and 0 (the empty string) before any. So `string s = "x";` gives `s` a wrong value, and no later `"x"` literal reuses it. id 1.01 declares no string constants. QC-27.12 diverges.
Global offsets 0 to 27 are reserved: 0 is null, 1 to 3 the return value, and 4 to 27 the eight three-word parameter slots. The first definition is at offset 28.

Every definition, temporary and literal takes the next free global offsets in the order the compiler meets them, its size from `QC_TYPE_SIZE`. A vector takes the three offsets of its `_x`, `_y` and `_z` definitions (QC-11.7).
A field definition's global holds its offset in the entity, in words. Field offsets are assigned from 0 in declaration order, a `.vector` taking three; the total is the progs' `entityfields`.

A function's `parm_start` is the offset of its first parameter and its `locals` count is the number of words from there to the end of the last `local` declaration in its body, including any temporaries allocated before that declaration; temporaries after the last `local` are not counted. A function with no `local` declaration has `locals` 0 even when it has parameters: 26 functions of id 1.01 do, `SUB_AttackFinished` among them.
Each operator, comparison or field load gets a new temporary that is never reused, not even across statements. Assignments, `IF`, `IFNOT`, `GOTO`, `RETURN`, `STATE` and calls get none.

A global definition is marked to be saved in saved games (`DEF_SAVEGLOBGAL`) when it is global, not initialised, and not a function or field. `qcc.h`: "All uninitialized globals will be saved to savegame files."
Each construct emits exactly the progs statements in the table below, in that order.
Branch operands are relative statement counts: `IF` and `IFNOT` carry the offset in operand b and `GOTO` in operand a, and the engine adds it to the index of the branch statement itself.
Operands a, b and c are signed 16-bit global offsets in the progs, as `dstatement_t` declares them; an unused operand is 0.
`qcc` reads `progs.src` from the current directory, or from the directory given with `-src`. It is a list of tokens: the first names the output file and each later one a source file.

Tokens are split as `COM_Parse` does: whitespace separates them; `//` starts a comment to the end of the line; `"..."` is one token without the quotes; each of `{`, `}`, `(`, `)`, `'` and `:` is a token of its own and ends a word. There are no `/* */` comments.
The source files are compiled in the order listed, as one program: each sees every definition of the files before it (QC-12.5). A file may be listed twice and is then compiled twice.
The output path is used as written, relative to the current directory, not to the `-src` directory; source paths are prefixed with the `-src` directory. id 1.01's `progs.src` names `../progs.dat`.
An empty `progs.src` is fatal, `No destination filename. qcc -help for info.` (with two spaces). A source file that cannot be opened is fatal.
Files that are in the source directory but not in `progs.src` are not part of the program (id 1.01 ships `amtest.qc`, `jctest.qc`, `models.qc` and `sprites.qc` this way).

The list ends at its first NUL byte outside a quoted token. `LoadFile` writes a NUL after the file's bytes (`buffer = SafeMalloc (length+1); ((byte *)buffer)[length] = 0;`), and `COM_Parse` takes any NUL for that end: one it meets between tokens (`if (c == 0) { com_eof = true; return NULL; }`), one that ends a word (`while (c>32)`) or a `//` comment (`while (*data && *data != '\n')`), each then met between tokens. So `progs.dat`, a NUL and `a.qc` list no file, and a word after the NUL is never read. A quoted token's loop tests only for the closing quote (`if (c=='\"')`), so it reads on past a NUL in it; the token is then a C string, and the name `main` opens is its text up to that NUL: `"a.qc` NUL `x" b.qc` lists `a.qc` and `b.qc`. The vanilla graph cases of `cargo xtask oracles builtins` hold these (`project-file.md` PRJ-4.11).

`COM_Parse` reads its text through `char *data` into `int c` and tests `while ( (c = *data) <= ' ')` and `} while (c>32);`, so on the x86 build, where `char` is signed, a byte of 0x80 to 0xFF is below the space, as QC-1.3 says of the lexer: it is white space between words and ends a word, and is kept only in a quoted word. So `progs.dat`, a line break and `b.qh` 0xE9 `x.qc` list `b.qh` and `x.qc`, and a UTF-8 `café.qc` is the word `caf` and then `.qc`. The vanilla graph cases of `cargo xtask oracles builtins` (`VANILLA_PROGS`) hold one, and the pinned id `qcc` compiles both files.

A quoted word's loop stops only at its closing quote (`if (c=='\"')`), so the word runs across line breaks, which it keeps: `"a.qc`, a line break and `b.qc"` is one name, which id's `qcc` fails to open. A quote the text ends in has no end: the loop reads on past `LoadFile`'s NUL and past the buffer, and the pinned build crashes (exit -10). This profile ends the list there with error `E0101` "EOF inside quote" at the line the quote opens on, a deliberate divergence. The vanilla graph cases (`VANILLA_PROGS`) hold both.
id's `qcc` has no warnings. Every diagnostic is an error, printed as `<file>:<line>:<message>` with the line of QC-1.5.
An error abandons the current top-level declaration. Recovery then skips tokens until it consumes a `;` at brace depth 0 and resumes parsing declarations after it.
Recovery re-lexes from the error position, so a lexical error can repeat; an unknown byte (QC-7.2) repeats until the error limit.
The error count runs across the whole compilation. When the 11th error is reported, the current file stops.
After a file that had any error, `qcc` exits with status 1 without compiling the remaining files.
After all files, every global function that was never defined is reported (QC-11.8) and compilation fails with the fatal error "compilation errors".

An error raised while lexing the first token of a file happens before the recovery point is set up; id's `qcc` jumps through an uninitialised `jmp_buf` and crashes. QC-27.1 makes it an ordinary error.
The output is a version 6 `progs.dat`. Statement 0, function 0, global definition 0, field definition 0 and string offset 0 (the empty string) are placeholders written before anything compiled.
Functions are numbered in the order their definitions finish parsing, from 1.

The global definitions table has one entry for every definition, in declaration order: globals, locals, parameters, `_x`/`_y`/`_z` components and `IMMEDIATE` literals, but not temporaries. Field definitions appear in both the field table (with the field's type) and the global table (with type field).

Strings are appended to the string table as they are met, never shared: each source file's name when the file starts, each string literal's text when its global is allocated, and each function's name when its definition finishes. Then, while writing, the name of every definition is appended once for the global table and once more for each field definition's entry in the field table. The table's length is rounded up to a multiple of 4.

`qcc` also writes `progdefs.h` in the current directory: a C `globalvars_t` with every global declared before the one named `end_sys_globals`, and an `entvars_t` with every field declared before the one named `end_sys_fields`, each element typed by its QuakeC type.

The progs header's `crc` is the 16-bit CRC (CCITT polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF, no final xor) of the text of `progdefs.h` up to the `#define` line, with LF line ends, as `qcc` reads it back. The engine refuses a progs whose CRC differs from its own `PROGHEADER_CRC`, 5927 for id's 1.01 system definitions (`PR_LoadProgs` in `WinQuake/pr_edict.c`: "progs.dat system vars have been modified, progdefs.h is out of date").

Writing `progdefs.h`, `qcc` assumes every vector definition before `end_sys_globals` is followed by its three component definitions. A vector literal (an `IMMEDIATE` with no components) before `end_sys_globals`, or the absence of `end_sys_globals` with any vector literal, makes it read past the end of the definition list; the reference build crashed. QC-27.13 diverges.

When the called function's name starts with `precache_sound`, `precache_model` or `precache_file`, the compile-time string value of the first argument's global is added to that list, once per distinct string.
The byte after the prefix chooses the pak block: `1` to `9` give that number (`precache_sound2` is block 2), anything else block 1.
A first argument that is not a constant adds the string at its global's compile-time value, normally the empty string.
`PrecacheModel` checks the sound count, not the model count, against its limit ("PrecacheModels: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS"), so the model list itself is unchecked.

A first argument whose compile-time word is no offset into the string table, such as a float's in `precache_model(1000000)`, adds nothing: id's `qcc` reads the string at that word (`n = G_STRING(e->ofs);`) outside its table, which C leaves undefined. This compiler keeps the lists without the limits of QC-26.4 and LIMIT-7.3, which bind id's `qcc` only.
A lexical error in the first token of a file is an ordinary error (QC-24.7).
A `/*` comment with no `*/` is an error, "unterminated comment", at the line of the `/*` (QC-2.4).
Keywords and punctuation are matched only against name and punctuation tokens; a string literal is always a string (QC-3.4).
A name, string literal or other token longer than `QC_MAX_TOKEN - 1` bytes is an error (QC-6.4).
A `,` or `;` on a `$frame` line is an error, and more than `LIMIT_QCC_MAX_FRAMES` frames in one file is an error (QC-8.9).
A frame name longer than `QC_MAX_FRAME_NAME` bytes is accepted and looked up by its full name, with a warning that id's `qcc` cannot use it (QC-8.9).
A function type with more than `LIMIT_MAX_PARMS` parameters is an error (QC-10.8).
An initialiser that is not a literal or frame macro reference is an error, "initialiser is not a constant" (QC-11.4).
`#0` and negative builtin numbers are errors (QC-13.4).

The left side of `=` must be a name or a field access; a literal, a call or an operator's result is an error, "cannot assign to this expression" (QC-17.2). Assigning to an initialised definition stays legal, as in id, with a warning (QC-11.6).
Only a field access on the left of `=` is turned into an address; an earlier statement's field load is never rewritten (QC-17.4).
A `string` initialiser stores the offset of its own text in the string table (QC-20.6).
`progdefs.h` generation skips component definitions only for vectors that have them (QC-25.7).

A `,` or `;` on a `$cd`, `$origin`, `$base`, `$flags`, `$scale` or `$skin` line makes id's `qcc` loop forever, as on a `$frame` line (QC-8.9). This compiler ignores the whole rest of such a line, `,` and `;` included (QC-8.4).

Constructs nested more than `QC_MAX_NESTING` levels deep are an error, "nesting too deep", at the token where the limit is passed. Each of these is one level inside the construct around it: a statement, a type, an expression (a whole statement's or initialiser's, a parenthesised one, the operand of `!`, a call argument, the right operand of a binary operator), and each binary operator, field access or call, which nests the expression before it one level deeper. id's `qcc` has no such limit; this compiler bounds the depth of its syntax tree so that no input can exhaust its stack.

Once the limit of QC-27.15 is passed in a statement or a declaration, no construct in it opens another level: the constructs it unwinds through read no further operator, field access, call or type around what they hold, so the tree stays within the limit, and the rest of the statement or declaration is skipped as after any error (QCD-1.4). The next statement or declaration nests afresh.

Each file's functions record the name `progs.src` lists the file by (QC-25.4), as id's `qcc` records it run in the source directory; `qcc -src DIR` records `DIR/` before it (`sprintf (filename, "%s%s", sourcedir, com_token)`).
A `string` initialiser's text (QC-27.12) is appended to the string table where the initialiser is read, and a later literal of the same text is the initialised definition (QC-20.2).

Every build writes a line map beside the progs, in FTEQCC's `.lno` layout ([`lno.md`](lno.md)), which id's `qcc` does not: one line per statement, the line of the source statement the compiler was reading when it emitted it, counted from 1 in the file the statement's function is in: a state header's statements have the line of the function's name, and the `DONE` a body ends with the line of its last statement (the name's for an empty body). The placeholder statement 0 has line 0, no line (LNO-3.2). The map's counts are the progs' (LNO-4.1).

With `--opt fold` (COMP-5), an arithmetic operator whose operands are both float or vector literals is the literal of its value, made as `PR_ParseImmediate` makes a literal (QC-20.2), and emits no statement: `ADD_F`, `SUB_F`, `MUL_F`, `DIV_F`, `ADD_V`, `SUB_V`, `MUL_V`, `MUL_FV` and `MUL_VF`. The value is the one the VM computes for that statement (VM-5): each product and sum an `f32` rounded in turn, the dot product `(a0*b0 + a1*b1) + a2*b2`, a division by zero infinity or NaN. Every other operator, and an operand that is no literal, is emitted as without the option. `qcc` folds nothing, so the option changes the progs but not what it computes (COMP-4).
A version 6 statement operand is a signed 16-bit value, so a statement can name global slots 0 to 32767 only (PROGS-7.2); a program with more globals cannot reach the rest from code.
A definition's `ofs` is unsigned 16-bit, so a definition can name global or field slots 0 to 65535 (PROGS-9.2).
A definition's type has 15 bits once `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` is removed: 0 to 32767.

A function has at most 8 parameters (`parm_size` has 8 entries and the call opcodes are `OP_CALL0` to `OP_CALL8`). Each parameter has 3 slots in the call area (PROGS-18.1), and qcc writes a `parm_size` of 1 or 3; the engine copies whatever `parm_size` says without checking it.

Entering a QC function adds one to the call depth, and the entry that makes the depth reach 32 fails with `stack overflow`. The function the engine calls counts, so at most 31 QC functions can be active at once.
The depth is shared by every QC function active in the engine, including those started by a nested `PR_ExecuteProgram` (for example a touch function run from inside a builtin).
Builtins do not count: calling a builtin does not enter a QC frame.

Entering a QC function saves its `locals` slots on a stack of 2048 slots shared by all active functions. An entry is allowed when the slots in use plus the new function's `locals` is at most 2048, and fails with `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack overflow` when it is more.

Each call of `PR_ExecuteProgram` has its own counter starting at 100000. The counter drops by one before each statement, and the statement that brings it to 0 fails with `runaway loop error` without executing, so one call executes at most 99999 statements.
Statements run by a nested `PR_ExecuteProgram` count against the nested call's own counter, not the outer one.
id's builtin table has 79 entries, numbers 0 to 78. Calling a function whose builtin number is 79 or more fails with `Bad builtin call number`.
Builtin 0 cannot be called: a `first_statement` of 0 is not negative, so the function runs statement 0 instead (PROGS-10.2).
A `first_statement` of -2147483648 has no positive builtin number; negating it overflows, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer as `Bad builtin call number`.

A server has at most 600 edicts, counting the world and the client edicts. When none can be reused and 600 are in use, allocating one (`spawn`, or an entity of the map being loaded) fails with `ED_Alloc: no free edicts`. Reuse rules are in [`edicts.md`](edicts.md) (EDICT-6).

The sound and model precache lists have 256 entries each, and entry 0 is always the empty string. Precaching a name already in the list does nothing; precaching a new name when all 256 entries are used fails with `PF_precache_sound: overflow` or `PF_precache_model: overflow`. So at most 255 sounds can be precached, and at most 255 models including the world model in entry 1 and its submodels after it.

qcc never checks its table sizes: more than 500000 bytes of strings, 65536 statements, 8192 functions, 16384 global definitions, 1024 field definitions or 16384 global slots overruns a fixed array, which is undefined in C. The result is not specified; a program that exceeds one does not build reliably with id's qcc.
A name of 63 or more characters fails with `name too long`, so a name has at most 62 characters.

qcc records the files named in `precache_sound`, `precache_model` and `precache_file` calls, 1024 of each. A new sound when 1024 are recorded fails with `PrecacheSound: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS`, and a new file when 1024 are recorded with `PrecacheFile: numfiles == MAX_FILES`. For models qcc tests the sound count instead (`PrecacheModels: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS`), so a new model fails only when 1024 sounds are recorded, and the 1025th model overruns its array.

FTEQCC writes a `.lno` for every compile unless the `filenames` optimisation is on (`if (!opt_filenames)` builds `statement_linenums`, otherwise it is `NULL` and nothing is written). That optimisation is off with no `-O` option (it lacks `FLAG_ASDEFAULT`) and on from `-O1` (its level is 1); `-flno` turns it back off with the warning "Disabling -Ofilenames to satisfy -flno request".
FTEQCC writes no `.lno` for its debug target (`QCF_FTEDEBUG`): that target stores the line table inside the progs (PROGS-21.1) and sets `statement_linenums = NULL` after doing so.

GMQCC writes a `.lno` only with `-flno`, which `-g` also turns on (`case 'g': opts_setflag("LNO", true)`), and only when it has exactly one line entry per statement (otherwise it prints `Linecounter wrong` and writes the progs without a `.lno`).

The `.lno` path is the output progs path with its last extension replaced by `.lno`: `progs.dat` gives `progs.lno`, `qwprogs.dat` gives `qwprogs.lno`. Both compilers append `.lno` to a name with no extension. FTEQCC also strips a trailing `.gz` first and appends it again (`progs.dat.gz` gives `progs.lno.gz`); a compressed `.lno` is outside this spec.

The readers look for the `.lno` beside the progs they load, by the same name rule (FTE `StripExtension` then `.lno`; DarkPlaces `FS_StripExtension` then `.lno`), through the game filesystem. A missing `.lno` is not an error: the progs runs without line numbers.
FTE reads a `.lno` only when the progs has no line table of its own: a version 7 file with `ofslinenums` not 0 (PROGS-21.1) uses that table and the `.lno` is not opened (`if (!pr_linenums)`).

A `.lno` starts with the 24-byte header above: the four bytes `LNOF` (0x4C 0x4E 0x4F 0x46), then five 32-bit little-endian integers. FTEQCC writes the magic as the bytes of `*(unsigned int*)"LNOF"` and GMQCC as `fwrite("LNOF", 4, 1, fp)`; both put the same four bytes in that order on a little-endian machine.

The only version any writer produces or any reader accepts is 1. FTE rejects any other value (`file[1] != version`), as DarkPlaces does (`LittleLong(header[1]) == 1`). There is no version 2: GMQCC's column table (LNO-3.3) is added without changing the version.

The four counts are copied from the progs written in the same compile: FTEQCC writes its globals `numglobaldefs`, `numpr_globals`, `numfielddefs` and `numstatements`, the same values it stores in `progs.numglobaldefs`, `progs.numglobals`, `progs.numfielddefs` and `progs.numstatements`; GMQCC writes `code_header.defs.length`, `globals.length`, `fields.length` and `statements.length`, the fields of the progs header it writes next.

GMQCC byte-swaps every value to little-endian before writing (`util_endianswap`). FTEQCC writes the counts and lines in host byte order with no swap, and FTE compares them unswapped. This spec reads and writes little-endian only, which is what both produce on the x86 and ARM hosts they run on; a file FTEQCC wrote on a big-endian host fails LNO-5.2 or LNO-4.1.

The line table follows the header: `numstatements` i32 values, the entry at index `i` being the source line of statement `i`. FTEQCC writes `statement_linenums`, an `int` array filled from `statements[i].linenum`; GMQCC writes `code->linenums`, a `std::vector<int>` with one entry pushed for every statement.

A line number is 1-based: both lexers start a file at line 1 (FTEQCC `pr_source_line = 1`; GMQCC "we start counting at 1"). FTEQCC takes the line of the last token read when the statement was emitted (`pr_token_line_last`), so a statement can carry the line of the token that ended the expression rather than the one that began it; FTEQCC's `#pragma line(n)` makes the following line `n`. The value 0 means the writer had no line: GMQCC's statement 0 (pushed with `empty_ctx`, line 0) and FTEQCC's global initialiser statements (`linenum = 0`, "the file won't be meaningful so nor will the line").

GMQCC writes a column table straight after the line table: `numstatements` i32 values from `code->columnnums`, one per statement, so its files are exactly `24 + 8 * numstatements` bytes. FTEQCC writes no column table, so its files are exactly `24 + 4 * numstatements` bytes.

A column is the value of GMQCC's lexer column counter when the statement's source context was taken: the counter is 0 at the start of each line, goes up by one for each byte `lex_fgetc` reads and down by one for each `lex_ungetch`, with an extra adjustment for multi-byte UTF-8 characters in string literals. The column of statement 0 is 0. This spec treats the value as GMQCC's own measure: it keeps it as written and does not convert it to a 1-based or character-based column.

Line and column values are stored as signed `int`; GMQCC narrows its `size_t` counters into them. No writer produces a negative value for an ordinary source file, but a reader keeps any i32 unchanged and does not reject negative values.

DarkPlaces reads the column table only when the file is strictly longer than `24 + 8 * numstatements` bytes (`filesize > (6 + 2 * numstatements) * sizeof(int)`), so it ignores the columns of a file GMQCC wrote, which is exactly that long. This spec deliberately differs (LNO-5.4): a file of at least that length has a column table, because that is the layout GMQCC writes.
No writer puts anything after the tables. FTE does not look at the file size at all and DarkPlaces checks only a minimum (LNO-5.3), so both ignore bytes after the tables.

A `.lno` belongs to a progs when all four counts equal that progs' header fields `numglobaldefs`, `numglobals`, `numfielddefs` and `numstatements` (PROGS-2.1), compared as unsigned 32-bit values (FTE compares `unsigned int` file words with the `int` header fields; DarkPlaces casts both sides to `unsigned int`). Both readers check exactly these four and nothing else: no CRC and no checksum of the progs.

When the counts do not match, the readers drop the `.lno` silently and run the progs without line numbers (FTE: "whoops: old progs or incompatible"). A reader of this spec reports the mismatch as a typed error naming the first field that differs, in header order, and leaves the decision to drop it to the caller.
A stale `.lno` whose counts happen to equal the new progs' passes LNO-4.1 and gives wrong lines; the format cannot detect it.

A `.lno` holds no file names. A statement's source file is the `s_file` of the function whose statements contain it (PROGS-10.1), as DarkPlaces prints it (`PRVM_GetString(prog, func->s_file)` beside `statement_linenums[statement]`). A function whose body includes code from another file therefore reports that code's lines against the function's own file.
Statement 0 and any statement outside every function have no file. Their line entries are still present and are kept as read.
A file shorter than 24 bytes is rejected with a typed error.
A file whose first four bytes are not exactly `LNOF` (case-sensitive) is rejected with a typed error.
A `version` other than 1 is rejected with a typed error carrying the version.

With `n` the header's `numstatements`, computed without overflow: a file shorter than `24 + 4n` bytes is rejected with a typed error (the line table is truncated). A file of at least `24 + 8n` bytes, with `n` above 0, has a column table of `n` entries after the line table. Otherwise there is no column table.
Bytes after the last table the file has (LNO-5.4) are trailing bytes. The reader does not reject them; it keeps them so that the writer can reproduce the file (LNO-6.2).
The checks run in the order LNO-5.1, LNO-5.2, LNO-5.3, LNO-5.4, and the first failure is reported. Reading a `.lno` does not need its progs; LNO-4.1 is a separate check on a file that has been read.
Reading never fails on the values: line and column values are kept as read (LNO-3.5), and the three counts other than `numstatements` are kept as read whatever they are.

The writer writes `LNOF`, version 1, `numglobaldefs`, `numglobals` and `numfielddefs` as given, `numstatements` as the length of the line table, the line table, the column table if there is one, then the trailing bytes if any. The output is `24 + 4n` bytes with no column table (FTEQCC's layout) and `24 + 8n` with one (GMQCC's), plus the trailing bytes.
A file the reader accepts is written back byte for byte, and reading what the writer wrote gives back the counts, tables and trailing bytes it was given.

The writer rejects, with a typed error and no output: a column table whose length differs from the line table's, a column table when the line table is empty (the reader would read it back as no column table, LNO-5.4), and a line table longer than 2147483647 entries (the largest `numstatements` PROGS-2.1's `i32` can hold).
The editor's compiler writes the three counts from the progs it writes in the same build, so that the result passes LNO-4.1 against that progs.
A file is read up to its first NUL byte or its end, whichever comes first.

Tokens are separated by whitespace: every byte from 0x01 to 0x20, and every byte from 0x80 to 0xFF. qbsp compares a `char`, signed on x86, with 32, so the high bytes count as whitespace there; this spec follows the x86 build. A CR before a LF is therefore whitespace, and lines are counted by LF.
`//` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. Comments separate tokens and may stand on their own lines or follow the last token of a line.

A `"` starts a quoted token that runs to the next `"`; the quotes are not part of it. It may be empty and may hold any byte but `"` and NUL, including a LF. A backslash is an ordinary byte: qbsp keeps `\n` as the two bytes `\` and `n`, and the engine decodes it when it spawns the entity (EXAMPLE-1). A file that ends inside a quoted token fails with the error `EOF inside quoted token`.
Any other token is a run of bytes up to the next whitespace. `(`, `)`, `{`, `}` and `"` do not end it, so `(0` is one token.
A token holds at most 127 bytes; a longer one fails with the error `Token too large on line <n>`.
Where a token must be on the current line (MAP-2.3, MAP-3.2, MAP-4.1), a LF, a comment or the end of the file before it fails with the error `Line <n> is incomplete`.

ericw-tools tokenises the same way except that it also takes `;` as the start of a comment, and inside a quoted token keeps a backslash and the byte after it as they are, so `\"` does not end the token unless a CR or LF follows it; it warns about escapes other than `\n`, `\'`, `\r`, `\t`, `\\`, `\b`, `\x` and `\0` to `\9`. A file that qbsp reads gives the same tokens in ericw-tools unless it holds `;` outside quotes or `\"` inside them.

The line number in qbsp's errors (`Line <n> is incomplete`, `Token too large on line <n>`) counts only the LFs `GetToken` skips between tokens (`if (*script_p++ == '\n') ... scriptline++;`). The LF that ends a `//` comment is consumed with the comment (`while (*script_p++ != '\n')`) and a LF inside a quoted token is copied into it, and neither is counted, so after a comment qbsp's line numbers fall behind the file's.

A file is zero or more entities. Each starts with the token `{`; any other token where an entity should start fails with the error `ParseEntity: { not found`. The end of the file between entities ends the list.

Inside an entity, the token `}` ends it, `{` starts a brush (MAP-3), and any other token is a key followed by its value. The end of the file inside an entity fails with the error `ParseEntity: EOF without closing brace`.
A value must be on the same line as its key (MAP-1.7). Keys and values are tokens, normally quoted; an unquoted word is accepted as either.
A key of 31 bytes or more, or a value of 1023 bytes or more, fails with the error `ParseEpar: token too long`. A value is in practice limited to 127 bytes by MAP-1.6.

An entity may have the same key more than once. qbsp keeps every pair and looks a key up by its last occurrence; ericw-tools keeps one pair per key, at the position of the first occurrence, holding the last value.

qbsp writes the entity lump with each entity's pairs in the reverse of their order in the `.map`, one `"key" "value"` per line, between `{` and `}` lines, and skips an entity with no pairs. Since the engine applies pairs in lump order with a later key overwriting an earlier one (EDICT-8.2), the game sees the first occurrence of a duplicated key when the map is compiled by qbsp.
The `origin` key, when present, is read as three numbers separated by whitespace, each as C `sscanf`'s `%lf`; missing or unreadable components are 0.
A map holds at most 1024 entities; the 1025th fails with the error `num_entities == MAX_MAP_ENTITIES`.
ericw-tools also removes whitespace from both ends of each key.

qbsp formats each pair as `"key" "value"` and a LF into a 128-byte buffer when it writes the entity lump (`WriteEntitiesToString`, `char line[128]`), so a pair whose key and value together exceed 121 bytes overflows it, which is undefined (a build with stack checks stops there). This spec fixes the answer: such a pair is reported as one id's qbsp cannot compile. ericw-tools has no such limit.
A brush is `{`, then faces, then `}`. Each face starts with `(` (any other token fails with the error `parsing brush`) and the end of the file ends the brush.

A face is three points, each `(`, three numbers and `)`. The three numbers and the `)` must be on the line of their `(`, but each point's `(` may start a new line. The texture definition follows on the line of the third point's `)` (MAP-4, MAP-5).
qbsp reads each point coordinate with C `atoi`, so `0.5` is 0 and a token that does not start with a number is 0; ericw-tools reads them as doubles.

The face's plane has the normal `normalize((p0 - p1) x (p2 - p1))` and the distance `dot(p1, normal)`. The brush is the region on the back of every face's plane, so each normal points out of the brush.

A face whose three points all lie within 0.05 units of an earlier face's plane is a duplicate: qbsp prints `WARNING: brush with duplicate plane` and drops it. The test ignores the plane's orientation, so a face on the same plane facing the other way is also dropped. ericw-tools drops it too.

A face whose points are collinear has no normal. qbsp prints `WARNING: brush plane with no normal` and stops reading the brush there, so the rest of the brush is then read as entity keys, which normally fails; ericw-tools warns and drops only that face. This spec's reader keeps the face and reports it.

After the points come six tokens on the same line: the texture name, the s and t shift, the rotation and the s and t scale. qbsp reads the shifts and rotation as integers (`atoi`) and the scales as floats; ericw-tools reads all five as doubles.

The base axes come from the plane's normal: the first of the six rows below whose axis has the largest dot product with the normal, compared with `>` so the earliest wins a tie (a normal with no positive dot product takes the floor row):

The axes are rotated by `rotate` degrees in the plane of the two non-zero axis components: with `sv` the index of the s axis's non-zero component and `tv` that of the t axis's, each axis `a` becomes `a[sv] = cos * a[sv] - sin * a[tv]` and `a[tv] = sin * a[sv] + cos * a[tv]` (using the old values). For 0, 90, 180 and 270 the sine and cosine are exactly 0 or 1 or -1; otherwise they are `sin` and `cos` of `rotate / 180 * pi`.
A scale of 0 is taken as 1. The texinfo's axes (BSP-8.1) are the rotated axes divided by their scale, and its offsets are the two shifts, unscaled.
qbsp sets `TEX_SPECIAL` (BSP-8.5) on the texinfo when the texture name starts with `*` or with `sky` in any case.

The texture name names a texture in the WAD2 files of MAP-6.3. qbsp copies it into a 16-byte slot, so a name of 16 bytes or more overflows it, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer: a name holds at most 15 bytes, as a WAD2 lump name (WAD-2).

qbsp gives each distinct texture name a slot in first-use order, and each distinct texinfo (texture, flags and the eight axis values compared exactly) one texinfo in first-use order. A map uses at most 4096 of each; the next fails with the error `nummiptex == MAX_MAP_TEXINFO` or `numtexinfo == MAX_MAP_TEXINFO`.

A Valve 220 face has, after the texture name, `[`, the s axis's x, y and z, the s shift, `]`, then `[`, the t axis and t shift, `]`, then the rotation and the s and t scale, all on the line of the third point; numbers are read as doubles. Any other token where a bracket belongs fails (`couldn't parse Valve220 texture info`).

ericw-tools decides the form face by face: a face whose token after the texture name is `[` is Valve 220, any other is standard. The worldspawn key `mapversion` with the value `220`, which editors write for this form, is not read.
The texinfo's axes are the given axes divided by their scale, and its offsets are the given shifts, unscaled. The rotation is not applied: it is kept for editors.
ericw-tools divides by a Valve 220 scale of 0, which gives an infinite or NaN axis; this spec fixes the answer: a scale of 0 in a Valve 220 face is an error.
id's qbsp does not read the Valve 220 form: it takes `[` as the first shift and then fails with the error `parsing brush`.

The first entity is the world. Its `classname` is `worldspawn` by convention; neither qbsp nor the engine checks it: qbsp builds the first entity's brushes into model 0 whatever its keys, and the engine spawns the first entity into edict 0 and calls the function its `classname` names (EDICT-4.2, EDICT-8.6).

Every later entity with at least one brush is a brush entity. qbsp numbers them in file order from 1 and sets each one's `model` key to `*<n>` (BSP-15.3), replacing any value the `.map` gave. An entity with no brushes keeps its keys as written.

qbsp reads its textures from the world's `_wad` key or, when that is missing or empty, its `wad` key: one path, relative to the game directory. With neither it prints `WARNING: no wadfile specified` and writes an empty textures lump. ericw-tools reads the same keys as a list of paths separated by `;`.
