Nothing is filled when `fillcolor` is `filledcolor` or 255.

A skin has four slots, `gl_texturenum[i][4]`. A single skin fills all four. A group's frame `j` goes in slot `j&3`, and after the loop `for (; j < 4; j++) gl_texturenum[i][j&3] = gl_texturenum[i][j - k]` with `k` the group's count. The slot drawn is `anim = (int)(cl.time*10) & 3`. GLQuake does not check the entity's `skinnum`; a skin the model does not have is drawn as skin 0 here, our choice.

A corner's skin coordinates are `s = stverts[k].s`, plus `skinwidth / 2` when the vertex is on the seam and the triangle does not face front, then `(s + 0.5) / skinwidth` and `(t + 0.5) / skinheight` (`BuildTris`). Strips join only triangles with the same `facesfront`, so this is the triangle's own. A skin is uploaded as a world texture is, `GL_LoadTexture (..., true, false)`: palette, resampling, mipmaps and filtering as REND-3.2 and REND-3.3, every pixel opaque.

A frame entry is one pose, or a group of poses whose `interval` is the group's *first* interval (`Mod_LoadAliasGroup`). The pose drawn is the frame's first, plus `(int)(cl.time / interval) % numposes` when it has more than one. A frame the model does not have draws frame 0 ("no such frame"). An interval of 0 or less is refused when the model loads (`Mod_LoadAliasGroup: interval<=0`); a NaN one, which loads, holds the first pose here, our choice: id's int conversion of a NaN quotient is undefined.

A vertex is at `v * scale + scale_origin` in the model (`glTranslatef (scale_origin)`, `glScalef (scale)`), turned and moved by `R_RotateForEntity`: roll about x, then `-angles[0]` about y, then yaw about z, then the origin. Unlike a brush model (REND-1.9) the pitch is not negated first.

**Withdrawn** 2026-10-30: it held every style at `REND_UNSET_STYLE`, which lightstyles now replace with their values; replaced by REND-4.10 and REND-5.6. `R_LightPoint (p)` is 255 in a map with no lighting lump. Otherwise it follows the line from `p` to 2048 units below it through the world's nodes from node 0: on a node it goes down the side `front < 0` of `start`, and when `end` is on the same side, only there; else to the crossing `mid = start + (end - start) * front/(front-back)`, then the node's faces, then the far side from `mid`. A face drawn tiled (sky, water) is skipped. For the others, `s` and `t` are the texinfo's dot products at `mid` with their offsets, truncated to ints; a face is hit when `s - texturemins[0]` and `t - texturemins[1]` are each from 0 to its extents. A face hit with no samples gives 0; one with samples gives `(sum over its styles of sample * style value) >> 8` at sample `(dt>>4) * ((extents[0]>>4)+1) + (ds>>4)`, every style at `REND_UNSET_STYLE`. A leaf hit with nothing gives 0.

`ambientlight` and `shadelight` start as `R_LightPoint (origin)`. `ambientlight` is capped at 128, and when `ambientlight + shadelight > 192`, `shadelight` becomes `192 - ambientlight`. Then `progs/flame2.mdl` and `progs/flame.mdl` are set to 256 ("make torches full light"), and `shadelight` is divided by 200. The view model's floor of 24, the players' floor of 8 and dynamic lights are not drawn yet.

The shade of a vertex is `shadedots[lightnormalindex] * shadelight`, with `shadedots` the row `((int)(angles[1] * (SHADEDOT_QUANT / 360.0))) & (SHADEDOT_QUANT - 1)` of `r_avertexnormal_dots`, 16 rows of 256 entries. It is given to `glColor3f`, so it is clamped to 0 to 1 before it is interpolated: OpenGL 1.1, 2.13.6, "After lighting (whether enabled or not), RGBA colors are clamped to the range [0, 1]." It is interpolated across the triangle (`gl_smoothmodels`, `GL_SMOOTH`), and the skin's colour is multiplied by it (`GL_MODULATE`).

A model whose header has `EF_ROTATE` (items and weapons) is drawn with yaw `bobjrotate = anglemod(100*cl.time)` (`CL_RelinkEntities`), with `anglemod (a)` of the float `a` being `(360.0/65536) * ((int)(a*(65536/360.0)) & 65535)`.

`R_LightPoint (p)` is 255 in a map with no lighting lump. Otherwise it follows the line from `p` to 2048 units below it through the world's nodes from node 0: on a node it goes down the side `front < 0` of `start`, and when `end` is on the same side, only there; else to the crossing `mid = start + (end - start) * front/(front-back)`, then the node's faces, then the far side from `mid`. A face drawn tiled (sky, water) is skipped. For the others, `s` and `t` are the texinfo's dot products at `mid` with their offsets, truncated to ints; a face is hit when `s - texturemins[0]` and `t - texturemins[1]` are each from 0 to its extents. A face hit with no samples gives 0; one with samples gives `(sum over its styles of sample * style value) >> 8` at sample `(dt>>4) * ((extents[0]>>4)+1) + (ds>>4)`, the style values as REND-5.6 says. A leaf hit with nothing gives 0.
There are 64 styles (`MAX_LIGHTSTYLES`). A face lists up to four, ended by 255 (`MAXLIGHTMAPS`).
A style with no string, or an empty one (`!cl_lightstyle[j].length`), is 256.

Otherwise its value at time `cl.time` is `(map[k] - 'a') * 22` with `k = (int)(cl.time*10) % length`, so `a` is 0, `m` ("normal light") 264 and `z` ("double bright") 550. A letter before `a` gives a negative value, as id's code does. A negative time makes id's `k` negative and reads before the string; this renderer reads the first letter then, our choice, since the result in id's code is undefined.

`d_lightstylevalue` is an `int` and `R_BuildLightMap`'s `scale` an `unsigned`, so the products and their sum are unsigned and wrap. The sum is then read into the signed `int t`, shifted right by 7 and capped at 255; GLQuake's luminance texture keeps `255 - t` as a byte, so the light drawn is the low byte of `t` when `t` is below 256, and 255 above it.

GLQuake rebuilds a face's lightmap when one of its styles' values differs from the value it was built with (`R_RenderBrushPoly`: `d_lightstylevalue[fa->styles[maps]] != fa->cached_light[maps]`). This renderer builds the whole atlas again in that case; the texels are the same.
`R_LightPoint` sums `sample * scale` with the same style values into the `int r`, so its products wrap the same way, and shifts it right by 8 (`RecursiveLightPoint`).

With a `.lit` file the samples of a face are its triples, from `lightdata + (lofs * 3)` ("lit support via lordhavoc"); without one, each byte of the lighting lump is its own red, green and blue ("expand the white lighting data to color").

Each channel is summed as REND-1.13 sums a texel, into an `unsigned` that wraps, shifted right by 7 (`r = *bl++ >> 7`) and capped at 255. The renderer draws a map without a `.lit` file as GLQuake does (REND-5.4), and one with it as QuakeSpasm does.

A sprite starts with a 36-byte header: `ident`, `version`, `type` as signed 32-bit integers, `boundingradius` as a float, `width`, `height` and `numframes` as signed 32-bit integers, `beamlength` as a float and `synctype` as a signed 32-bit integer.
A sprite's first four bytes are `IDSP` (0x49 0x44 0x53 0x50). A file that does not start with them is not a sprite: the engine loads it as another kind of model, and the sprite reader rejects it.
`version` must be 1; any other value fails with the error `<name> has wrong version number (<version> should be 1)` (fatal in id's engine).
`numframes` must be at least 1; 0 or a negative value fails with the error `Mod_LoadSpriteModel: Invalid # of frames: <numframes>` (fatal in id's engine).

`type`, `boundingradius`, `width`, `height`, `beamlength` and `synctype` are not checked when the sprite loads. A `type` other than 0 to 4 loads and fails only when the sprite is drawn (`R_DrawSprite: Bad sprite type <type>` in `WinQuake/r_sprite.c`, `R_DrawSprite`); the frames are not checked against `width` and `height`.
A file shorter than the 36-byte header fails to load. id's code reads the header from the loaded buffer without checking its length, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

The model's bounds are `mins = (-width / 2, -width / 2, -height / 2)` and `maxs = (width / 2, width / 2, height / 2)` with C integer division, which truncates toward zero, so a width of 33 gives -16 and 16. The negation comes before the division and wraps as on x86, so a width of -2147483648 gives -1073741824 for both.

After the header come `numframes` frame entries, each starting with a 32-bit frame type. A type of 0 (`SPR_SINGLE`) is followed by one frame; any other value, not only 1 (`SPR_GROUP`), is followed by a frame group.

A frame is a 16-byte `dspriteframe_t` (`origin[0]`, `origin[1]`, `width`, `height`) followed by `width * height` bytes of palette indices, row by row from the top left. The next entry starts right after the pixels.
A frame's extents are `up = origin[1]`, `down = origin[1] - height`, `left = origin[0]` and `right = width + origin[0]`, computed in 32-bit integers that wrap as on x86.

A frame with a negative `width` or `height`, whose `width * height` does not fit in a 32-bit signed integer, or whose header or pixels run past the end of the file, fails to load. id's code copies `width * height` bytes without checking them, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
A frame group is a 32-bit `numframes`, then `numframes` float intervals, then `numframes` frames as in SPR-2.2, with no frame type before each.
Every interval must be greater than 0; one that is 0 or less fails with the error `Mod_LoadSpriteGroup: interval<=0` (fatal in id's engine). The test is `interval <= 0.0`, so a NaN interval loads.

A frame group's `numframes` must be at least 1. id's code loads a group of 0 frames, and `R_GetSpriteframe` then reads the interval before the group's array, which is undefined; a negative count fails in id's `Hunk_AllocName`. This spec fixes both as an error.
An interval or frame of a group that runs past the end of the file fails to load, as in SPR-2.4.
Bytes after the last frame entry are ignored.
A trace is one header (TRACE-2) followed by zero or more records (TRACE-4), in the order the events they describe happened. It has no end marker: it ends after its last complete record.
The binary form (TRACE-5) and the JSON form (TRACE-6) hold the same information. Decoding either form and encoding the result in the other, then decoding that, gives back the same header and records.

The header is written after the progs is loaded (its globals hold the values the file gives them) and before the first run. Every run the host starts after that is traced, including runs nested inside builtins (VM-18).

Globals are named by slot number, edicts by edict number (0 is the world) and entity fields by field slot number (PROGS-13), never by an address or an entity value, so the names do not depend on how a VM lays out its memory. Values are the raw 32-bit patterns of the slots (PROGS-17.1), written exactly, NaN payloads included.

The header holds the format version and five numbers: `progs_crc`, the CRC of the whole progs.dat file (PROGS-6.1, id's `pr_crc`), so a reader can check that two traces ran the same file; `edict_size`, the bytes between the entity values of consecutive edicts in this VM (id's `pr_edict_size`); `field_offset`, the bytes from an entity value to the pointer value of its field slot 0; `entityfields`, the number of field slots per edict (the progs header's `entityfields`); and `numstrings`, the size of the loaded string table in bytes.
The version is `TRACE_VERSION`. A reader rejects any other version: a change to the format that an old reader would misread is a new version.

`edict_size` is at least 1, `progs_crc` fits in 16 bits, and the fields fit inside an edict: `field_offset + 4 * entityfields` is at most `edict_size`, computed without overflow. A reader rejects a header that breaks any of these, and an emitter cannot write one.

A change set lists every global slot and every entity field slot whose 32-bit pattern, at the moment the record is written, differs from its pattern when the previous change-carrying record was written, or, for the first one, when the header was written. The patterns are compared as bits, so `-0.0` differs from `0.0` and a NaN equals itself only when its bits do.
Each slot appears at most once, with its value at the moment the record is written. A slot that changed and then changed back to its earlier pattern is not listed.
Global changes are in ascending order of slot. Field changes are in ascending order of edict number, and of field slot within one edict.

The globals compared are slots 0 to `numglobals - 1`. The fields compared are slots 0 to `entityfields - 1` of every edict the VM has in use (in id's engine edicts 0 to `sv.num_edicts - 1`), free or not. An edict that was not in use at the previous change-carrying record is compared against all-zero fields, so a newly allocated edict lists only its non-zero fields.

Only the globals and the fields are compared. The call stack, the local stack, the runaway counter, `pr_argc` and whether an edict is free are not in a change set; the differences they make show up in later globals and fields, or in the records' order.

A run record is written when the host or a builtin calls `PR_ExecuteProgram`, before any of the checks of VM-2. It holds the function index as passed, a signed 32-bit number, and a change set: for a run started by the host, the host's own changes since the previous record (setting `self` and `time`, spawning edicts); for a nested run, what the builtin changed before starting it.

A step record is written when a statement finishes without an error. It holds the index of the function that was current when the statement became current (VM-3.1), before any call or return the statement makes; the statement's index; its opcode as the statement stores it (PROGS-7.1); the builtin number when there is one (TRACE-4.3); and a change set.

A step record has a builtin number exactly when its statement is a `CALL0` to `CALL8` that called a builtin (VM-14.4): the number `-first_statement` of the function it called. The step's change set includes what the builtin wrote, `OFS_RETURN` among it.

When a builtin starts nested runs, each run's records (its run record, its statements' records and its exit or error record) are written while the builtin is running, so they come before the step record of the `CALL` that called the builtin. That step record's change set holds what the builtin changed after the last nested run returned.

An exit record is written when `PR_ExecuteProgram` returns to its caller (VM-16.4). It holds only a change set, which is normally empty: the `DONE` or `RETURN` that ended the run has its own step record.

An error record is written instead of a step record when a runtime error ends the run (VM-19.1, VM-19.7), and also for the errors a run raises before its first statement (VM-2.1, VM-2.2, VM-2.4). It holds a function index, a statement index, the message and a change set (VM-19.5 says what a failed statement may already have written).

For an error raised by a statement, an error record's function and statement are the ones `PR_RunError` prints (VM-19.1): the current function and statement, so for `runaway loop error` the statement before the one that was not run. For an error raised before a run's first statement (VM-2.1, VM-2.2, VM-2.4), the function is the index the run was given and the statement is -1.

An error record's message is the error's text as [`vm.md`](vm.md) gives it, without a trailing newline (`Bad opcode 70`, `NULL function`); for the errors of VM-19.7, which have no message in id's code, it is the implementation's own text. It contains no NUL byte.
After an error record, no record follows for any run that was active when the error happened (VM-19.2). The host may then start a new run, which begins with its own run record.

A string record is written whenever the VM makes a string value that lies outside the string table (PROGS-11.6) name some text: when a builtin or the host allocates an engine string, and whenever the text at such a value changes (id's `ftos`, `vtos` and `etos` all write `pr_string_temp` in `WinQuake/pr_cmds.c`). It holds the 32-bit string value and the text up to, not including, its NUL. It is written before the change-carrying record whose change set first shows the value, and it carries no change set: it does not reset what the next change set compares against (TRACE-3.1).

Numbers are written in three ways. A *word* is 4 bytes, little-endian. A *uvar* is an unsigned 32-bit number in LEB128: 7 bits per byte, least significant group first, the high bit set on every byte but the last. A *svar* is a signed 32-bit number `n` written as the uvar of its zigzag form, `(n << 1) ^ (n >> 31)` with an arithmetic shift, so 0, -1, 1, -2 become 0, 1, 2, 3.

A uvar is at most 5 bytes and uses the fewest bytes that hold its value: a reader rejects a uvar that runs past 5 bytes, one whose fifth byte is above 0x0F (the value would not fit in 32 bits), and one with more than one byte whose last byte is 0x00.
*Text* is a uvar byte count followed by that many bytes, none of them NUL.
The header is 28 bytes: the magic `QCTR` (0x51 0x43 0x54 0x52), then six words: the version, `progs_crc`, `edict_size`, `field_offset`, `entityfields` and `numstrings`.

A change set is a uvar count of global changes, each a uvar slot and a word holding the slot's bits, then a uvar count of field changes, each a uvar edict number, a uvar field slot and a word holding the bits.
Each record is a tag byte followed by its fields, in this order:

A reader rejects a stream that is shorter than the header or has the wrong magic, a record that ends before its last field, an unknown tag, a builtin flag byte other than 0x00 or 0x01, an opcode above 65535, and a change set that breaks the order of TRACE-3.3 or lists a slot twice. Because every value has exactly one encoding, encoding what a reader accepted gives back the same bytes.
The JSON form is JSON Lines: one JSON object per line, each line ended by a line feed (0x0A), the header on the first line and one record on each line after it. There are no blank lines.
The header is `{"trace":"qc-trace","version":1,"progs_crc":N,"edict_size":N,"field_offset":N,"entityfields":N,"numstrings":N}`.

A record's `t` key names it: `run`, `step`, `exit`, `error` or `string`. A run has `function`; a step has `function`, `statement`, `opcode` and, only when it has one, `builtin`; an error has `function`, `statement` and `message`; a string has `value` and `text`. Every change-carrying record also has `globals`, an array of `[slot, bits]`, and `fields`, an array of `[edict, field, bits]`, each empty when there are no changes. Numbers are JSON integers.
A 32-bit pattern (`bits`, and a string record's `value`) is a JSON string of exactly 8 lowercase hexadecimal digits: `"3f800000"` is 1.0.

Text (`message`, `text`) is a JSON string in which each byte from 0x20 to 0x7E other than the backslash stands for itself, and every other byte, the backslash included, is the four characters `\x` and two lowercase hexadecimal digits. In the JSON source the backslash is itself escaped, so the text `a\b` followed by a line feed is `"a\\x5cb\\x0a"`.

A writer puts the keys in the order TRACE-6.2 and TRACE-6.3 list them (`t` first), with no whitespace, and escapes text with JSON's own escapes only where RFC 8259 requires them (`\"` and `\\`). A reader accepts any key order and any JSON whitespace within a line, and rejects a missing key, an unknown key, a value of the wrong JSON type, a number out of range for its field, bits or text not written as TRACE-6.4 and TRACE-6.5 say, and the violations of TRACE-2.3 and TRACE-5.7 that the JSON form can express.
A 32-bit pattern read as a signed number `v` is the entity value of edict `n` when `v` is `n * edict_size` exactly, with `n` 0 or more. 0 is the world in every trace.
A pattern `v` is the pointer to field slot `f` of edict `n` when `v` is `n * edict_size + field_offset + 4 * f` exactly, with `n` 0 or more and `f` from 0 to `entityfields - 1`.

A string value `v` from 0 to `numstrings - 1` is an offset into the string table, the same in every trace of one progs. Any other string value names the text of the latest string record for `v` before the point being read, and no text if there is none.

The VM state is the globals (PROGS-12), the edicts, a call stack of frames (each the statement to return to and the function it belongs to), the call depth, a local stack of `LIMIT_LOCALSTACK_SIZE` slots and the number of them in use, the current function, the current statement and the argument count of the last call (`pr_argc`). All of it persists from one `PR_ExecuteProgram` call to the next; only the runaway counter belongs to one call (VM-2.3).
Execution reads the statements and functions tables and never writes them, except each function's `profile` counter (VM-3.1).

Each opcode uses its operands as VM-3.6 says. An operand used as a global slot names one slot for a scalar and the three slots `n`, `n+1`, `n+2` for a vector; an opcode reads and writes only the slots its section names. An operand the opcode does not use is ignored, whatever its value.

id's VM checks no operand: `PARANOID` is commented out in `quakedef.h`, so a global slot outside `0` to `numglobals - 1` is read or written outside the globals, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: a statement that would read or write a global slot outside that range fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) before it changes any global or field. It is a deliberate divergence; qcc never writes such an operand.

A function index of 0, or not less than `numfunctions`, fails with `PR_ExecuteProgram: NULL function`. This error goes straight to `Host_Error`, not through `PR_RunError`: no statement or stack trace is printed, the call depth is not reset, and when the global `self` is not 0 the engine prints that entity first.

A negative function index passes id's test (`!fnum || fnum >= numfunctions`) and reads before the start of the functions table, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails as VM-2.1 does.

A run sets its own runaway counter to `LIMIT_RUNAWAY` (LIMIT-4.1), clears the statement trace flag (`pr_trace`, set by the `traceon` builtin), records the current call depth as its exit depth, and enters the function as VM-15 says. It returns to its caller when a return brings the call depth back to the exit depth (VM-16.4).

A builtin (`first_statement` below 0) passed to `PR_ExecuteProgram` is entered as if it were a QC function, and execution starts at the negative statement index `first_statement`, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) before any statement runs. The engine never does this with id's progs.

Each step of the loop moves to the next statement (the current one plus one), decrements the runaway counter and, if it reaches 0, fails with `runaway loop error` without executing the statement (LIMIT-4.1). Otherwise it adds one to the current function's `profile`, makes the statement current and executes it.

Nothing marks the end of a function: execution runs on into the next statement in the table, whichever function it belongs to, until a `DONE` or `RETURN` (VM-16), a jump (VM-13) or a call (VM-14) moves it.

Reaching a statement index outside `0` to `numstatements - 1` (by running past the last statement, by a jump, or through a function's `first_statement`) reads outside the statements table, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) before the statement executes.
An opcode above 65 fails with `Bad opcode <op>`, the opcode printed as an unsigned decimal number (PROGS-7.4). The step has already counted against the runaway counter and `profile`.
Statement 0 is reserved and all zero (PROGS-1.5), so executing it is `DONE 0 0 0`: a jump to statement 0, or a function whose `first_statement` is 0 (LIMIT-5.2), returns at once.
The operands of each opcode are:

`c = a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b` or `a / b` in IEEE 754 single precision with round-to-nearest-even, the result rounded to f32 once. Subnormal operands and results are kept, not flushed to zero, and signed zeros follow IEEE 754 (`-0 - +0` is `-0`).

No arithmetic opcode fails. Overflow gives an infinity; a non-zero finite value divided by zero gives an infinity whose sign is the exclusive or of the operands' signs (so `1 / -0` is `-inf`); `0 / 0`, `inf - inf`, `inf / inf` and `0 * inf` give a NaN; and any NaN operand gives a NaN.

The sign and payload of a NaN that an operation produces are not specified: C leaves them to the CPU, and they differ between hosts (x86 produces 0xFFC00000 for `0 / 0`, ARM 0x7FC00000). An implementation may produce any NaN, and comparing a result with an expected value treats every NaN as equal to every other NaN. Copying a NaN never changes it (VM-10.3).
`c` may be the same slot as `a` or `b`: both operands are read before `c` is written.

`ADD_V` and `SUB_V` compute `c[i] = a[i] + b[i]` (or `-`) for `i` = 0, 1, 2 in that order, each component as VM-4.1. Each component reads its operands after the previous component's result is written, so when `c` overlaps `a` or `b` shifted by one or two slots, later components see the values just written. The C writes the components in this order, but because the operands are then partially overlapping objects a compiler may reorder the reads (GCC at `-O2` does unless given `-fno-strict-aliasing`); this spec fixes the source order.

`MUL_V` is the dot product: `c = (a[0]*b[0] + a[1]*b[1]) + a[2]*b[2]`, three products and two sums, each rounded to f32 as VM-4.1, added left to right, with no fused multiply-add. All six inputs are read before the one result slot is written. id's x87 build kept the intermediate values at a higher precision and could differ in the last bit; this spec fixes per-operation f32 rounding, which every SSE and ARM build gives when compiled without contraction (`-ffp-contract=off`).
`MUL_FV` computes `c[i] = a * b[i]` for `i` = 0, 1, 2 in order, reading the float `a` again for each component, so when `c[0]` is `a`'s slot the later components use the new value.
`MUL_VF` computes `c[i] = b * a[i]` for `i` = 0, 1, 2 in order, reading the float `b` again for each component in the same way.
`EQ_F`, `NE_F`, `LE`, `GE`, `LT` and `GT` write `1.0` to `c` when `a == b`, `a != b`, `a <= b`, `a >= b`, `a < b` or `a > b` holds for the floats, and `0.0` when it does not.

The comparisons are IEEE 754's: `-0` equals `+0`, and a NaN is unordered with everything including itself, so `EQ_F`, `LE`, `GE`, `LT` and `GT` give `0.0` and `NE_F` gives `1.0` when either operand is a NaN.

`EQ_V` gives `1.0` when all three components are equal as VM-6.2 says, and `NE_V` gives `1.0` when any component is unequal; a NaN in any component makes `EQ_V` `0.0` and `NE_V` `1.0`, even comparing a vector with itself.
All inputs are read before `c` is written, so `c` may overlap `a` or `b`.

`EQ_S` compares the two strings by content with `strcmp`: the bytes from each string value's offset up to its NUL (PROGS-11.1), compared as unsigned bytes. It writes `1.0` when they are equal. Different offsets holding the same text are equal, and offset 0 equals every empty string.

`NE_S` writes `strcmp`'s result converted to float: `0.0` when the strings are equal, otherwise the first differing byte of `a` minus that of `b`, both as unsigned bytes, the NUL at the end of the shorter string counting as 0. C fixes only the sign of `strcmp`; this spec fixes the byte difference, which glibc and macOS's C library return. Code that only tests the result for zero is unaffected.

A string value is an offset into the string table or a string the engine allocated (PROGS-11.6). `EQ_S`, `NE_S` and `NOT_S` resolve both: a value from 0 to `numstrings - 1` reads the string table (PROGS-11.1), and any other value reads the engine-allocated string it names (EDICT-13.1), id's `PR_GetString` computing `pr_strings + value` for either. Only a value that is neither a table offset nor an engine-allocated string names memory outside both, which is undefined in C; this spec fixes the answer: `EQ_S`, `NE_S` and `NOT_S` with such a value fail with a runtime error (VM-19.7).

`EQ_E` and `NE_E` compare the 32-bit patterns of `a` and `b`, and `EQ_FNC` and `NE_FNC` compare them as function indices, writing `1.0` or `0.0`. None of them checks that the value names an entity or function, and `EQ_E` compares bits, not floats: `-0.0` and `0.0` differ, and a NaN pattern equals itself.
`NOT_F` writes `1.0` when the float `a` equals `0.0` (so for `+0` and `-0`) and `0.0` otherwise, including for a NaN.
`NOT_V` writes `1.0` when all three components of `a` equal `0.0`.

`NOT_S` writes `1.0` when the string value is 0 or names an empty string (its first byte is NUL), and `0.0` otherwise. It resolves the value the same way `EQ_S` does (VM-7.3): a table offset reads the string table, and a value outside the table reads the engine-allocated string it names (PROGS-11.6, EDICT-13.1), so an engine-made string is false only when its text is empty (EDICT-13.2); a value that is neither fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7).
`NOT_ENT` writes `1.0` when the entity value is 0, the world, and `0.0` otherwise. It compares the value only, without checking that it names an edict or whether that edict is free.
`NOT_FNC` writes `1.0` when the function index is 0.
`AND` writes `1.0` when the floats `a` and `b` are both non-zero, and `OR` when either is. A NaN is non-zero and `-0` is zero. Both operands are always read; C's short-circuit has no visible effect.

These opcodes read their operands as floats, unlike `IF` and `IFNOT` (VM-13.3), which test the 32-bit pattern: a slot holding `-0.0` is false for `NOT_F`, `AND` and `OR` but true for `IF`. An integer value read as a float (a string offset, an entity value) is zero only when its pattern is 0x00000000 or 0x80000000.

`BITAND` and `BITOR` convert each float operand to a 32-bit signed integer by truncation toward zero, take the two's complement AND or OR, and write the integer converted back to float, rounded to nearest even, so a result above 2^24 can lose its low bits.

Converting a NaN, an infinity or a value whose truncation is outside -2^31 to 2^31 - 1 is undefined in C. This spec fixes the result of the conversion as -2147483648 (0x80000000), the value an x86 build produces: the "integer indefinite" result of SSE's `cvttss2si` and of the x87 `fist` instructions. An ARM build gives a different value (it saturates, and a NaN becomes 0), so an oracle run of these vectors is on x86.
Negative operands work in two's complement: `-8 | 3` is `-5` and `-1 & 5` is `5`.
`STORE_F`, `STORE_S`, `STORE_ENT`, `STORE_FLD` and `STORE_FNC` copy the 32-bit pattern of slot `a` to slot `b`. They are the same operation: the type in the name is not checked.

`STORE_V` copies slots `a`, `a+1`, `a+2` to `b`, `b+1`, `b+2` one at a time in that order. When `b` is `a+1` or `a+2` a later copy reads a slot already written, so `STORE_V 100 101` sets slots 101 to 103 to the old value of slot 100. This is the source order, fixed as in VM-5.1.

Every copy is bit-exact, including `-0.0` and every NaN pattern, signalling NaNs among them. `STORE_V` copies through float assignments in C, which id's x87 build may have done by loading and storing through the FPU, quietening a signalling NaN; this spec fixes the bit-exact copy, which no QC arithmetic can tell apart because no arithmetic produces a signalling NaN.
In a store, `b` is the destination and `c` is unused, unlike the other opcodes, which write their result to `c`.

`LOAD_F`, `LOAD_S`, `LOAD_ENT`, `LOAD_FLD` and `LOAD_FNC` take an entity value in `a` (PROGS-17.4) and a field index in `b` (PROGS-17.5), and copy the 32-bit pattern of that entity's field slot `b` to slot `c`. They are the same operation.
`LOAD_V` copies the entity's field slots `b`, `b+1`, `b+2` to `c`, `c+1`, `c+2`.
A load works on any edict: the world and free edicts are read like any other.

id does not check the entity value or the field index (`PARANOID` is off), so a value that does not name an edict, or a field slot outside `0` to `entityfields - 1`, reads other memory, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: such a load fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7). Which entity values name an edict is EDICT-1.9.

`ADDRESS` takes an entity value in `a` and a field index in `b` and writes to `c` a pointer to that entity's field slot `b` (PROGS-17.7). In id's engine the pointer is the entity value plus the byte offset of the fields within an edict plus `4 * b`; the offset is engine-specific (`edicts.md`), so only `STOREP` gives a pointer meaning.

`ADDRESS` on the world (entity value 0) fails with `assignment to world entity` while the server is active (`sv.state == ss_active`). While a map is loading (`ss_loading`, when spawn functions run) it succeeds.
`ADDRESS` reads no field and checks neither the field index nor whether the edict is free.

`STOREP_F`, `STOREP_S`, `STOREP_ENT`, `STOREP_FLD` and `STOREP_FNC` copy the 32-bit pattern of slot `a` to the field slot that the pointer in slot `b` names; `STOREP_V` copies slots `a` to `a+2` to that field slot and the next two, in order.

id writes wherever the pointer leads, which is undefined in C when it is not a field slot of an edict. This spec fixes the answer: a `STOREP` whose pointer does not name a field slot of an edict, or for `STOREP_V` three consecutive field slots of one edict, fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) without writing.
`STOREP` does not check for the world or a free edict: a pointer to a world field made while loading still writes to the world when the server is active.
`GOTO` makes the next statement the current one plus `a`, a signed offset (PROGS-7.2).
`IF` makes the next statement the current one plus `b` when the 32-bit pattern in slot `a` is not zero, and the current one plus one otherwise. `IFNOT` jumps by `b` when the pattern is zero.
The test is on the 32-bit pattern, not on the float: `-0.0` (0x80000000) and every NaN are true, and a string value is true when its offset is not 0, even if the string it names is empty.
An offset of 0 jumps to the same statement, so `GOTO 0` repeats until the runaway guard stops it (VM-3.1).
A jump outside the statements table is VM-3.3's error.

`CALL0` to `CALL8` call the function whose index is in slot `a`. The call sets the argument count (`pr_argc`), which builtins read, to the number in the opcode name. The arguments are already in the parameter slots `OFS_PARM0` to `OFS_PARM7` (PROGS-18.1), written by earlier statements; the call itself moves nothing.
A function index of 0 fails with `NULL function`.
id reads `pr_functions[index]` without checking, so a negative index or one not less than `numfunctions` is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7).

When the function is a builtin (`first_statement` below 0, PROGS-10.2), its number is `-first_statement`; a number of `LIMIT_NUM_BUILTINS` or more fails with `Bad builtin call number` (LIMIT-5.1, LIMIT-5.3). Otherwise the builtin is called directly: no frame is pushed, the call depth does not change (LIMIT-2.3), no locals are saved and no parameters are copied. A builtin returns a value by writing `OFS_RETURN`. When it returns, execution continues with the statement after the call.
When the function is a QC function it is entered as VM-15 says, and execution continues at its `first_statement`. The statement after the call runs when it returns (VM-16.4).

The number in the opcode is not checked against the callee's `numparms`: the callee copies `numparms` parameters from the parameter slots whatever they hold, including values left there by earlier calls.

Entering pushes a frame holding the current statement and the current function, and adds one to the call depth; when the new depth is `LIMIT_MAX_STACK_DEPTH` or more it fails with `stack overflow` (LIMIT-2.1). The depth is checked before the local stack.

Next it saves the callee's `locals` slots, from `parm_start` up, onto the local stack above the slots in use. When the slots in use plus `locals` is more than `LIMIT_LOCALSTACK_SIZE` it fails with `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack overflow` before saving anything (LIMIT-3.1).

Then it copies the parameters: with `o` starting at `parm_start`, for each parameter `i` from 0 to `numparms - 1` and each `j` from 0 to `parm_size[i] - 1`, slot `4 + 3*i + j` is copied to slot `o` and `o` goes up by one. Parameters are packed: a float parameter after a vector parameter lands at `parm_start + 3`. The copy comes after the save, so the saved values are the caller's.

`parm_size` is not checked: a size above 3 reads on past the parameter's three slots into the next parameter's, and past slot 27 into ordinary globals. A `numparms` of 0 or less copies nothing (PROGS-10.5).
The callee becomes the current function and execution continues at its `first_statement`.

A negative `locals` makes id move the local stack's top down, and a later entry or return writes outside it, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: entering a function whose `locals` is negative fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7). A save, restore or parameter copy that reaches a global slot outside the globals is VM-1.4's error.

Entering does not clear the local slots: a local that is not a parameter starts with whatever value its global slot held, normally the value left by the caller or by the last function that used the slot.

`DONE` and `RETURN` are the same operation. They copy slots `a`, `a+1`, `a+2` to `OFS_RETURN` (slots 1, 2, 3), one slot at a time in that order. All three are copied, even for a function returning a float or nothing.

qcc ends every function with `DONE 0 0 0`, so falling off the end copies slot 0 to slot 1, then slot 1 (now slot 0's value) to slot 2, then slot 2 to slot 3: all three return slots get slot 0's value, normally 0. A function that returns nothing therefore clears the return slots.

After the copy, the current function's `locals` slots are restored from the top of the local stack to `parm_start` up, the slots in use drop by `locals`, and the frame is popped: the current function and statement become the ones the frame saved. The return value is copied before the restore, so a function can return one of its own locals.

When the call depth is then back at the exit depth of the current run (VM-2.3), `PR_ExecuteProgram` returns to its caller. Otherwise execution continues with the statement after the call in the restored function.
The return copy is bit-exact, as VM-10.3 fixes for `STORE_V`.

`PR_LeaveFunction`'s own checks, `prog stack underflow` (through `Sys_Error`) and `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack underflow`, cannot fail: every return matches an entry of the same function, and `locals` is never negative (VM-15.6).

`STATE` acts on the entity in the global `self`. It sets that entity's `nextthink` field to the global `time` plus 0.1, added in double precision: `(float)((double)time + 0.1)`, where 0.1 is the double nearest to 0.1, not the float.

It sets the entity's `frame` field to the float in `a` only when that float is not equal to the current `frame` as VM-6.2 compares: when `a` is `-0.0` and `frame` is `+0.0`, or the reverse, `frame` keeps its bits, and when `a` is a NaN `frame` becomes that NaN.
It sets the entity's `think` field to the 32-bit pattern in `b`, a function index that is not checked.

`STATE` does not check for the world: with `self` 0 it writes the world's fields. A `self` that does not name an edict is VM-11.4's error. Where `self`, `time`, `nextthink`, `frame` and `think` are is in `edicts.md`; in id's `progdefs.q1` they are global slots 28 and 31 and field slots 46, 30 and 44.
A nested run shares the call stack, the call depth, the local stack and the globals with the outer run, and has its own runaway counter and exit depth (LIMIT-2.2, LIMIT-4.2).

When the nested run returns, the current function and statement are again the outer function and its call statement, restored from the frame the nested entry pushed; the builtin then returns and the outer run continues with the statement after the call.
A nested run clears the statement trace flag (VM-2.3), so tracing started before it is off after it.
An error in a nested run ends every run, not only the nested one (VM-19.2).

A runtime error from the VM (`stack overflow`, `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack overflow`, `runaway loop error`, `NULL function`, `Bad builtin call number`, `Bad opcode <op>`, `assignment to world entity`), like one from a builtin, goes through `PR_RunError`. It prints the current statement (the last one VM-3.1 made current, so for `runaway loop error` the statement before the one that was not run), then the call stack from the innermost function out as `<file> : <function>`, then the message; it sets the call depth to 0 ("dump the stack so host_error can shutdown functions") and calls `Host_Error ("Program error")`.
`Host_Error` ("This shuts down both the client and server") never returns: no further statement of any run executes, at any level of nesting, and `PR_ExecuteProgram` does not return to its caller.
**Withdrawn** 2026-10-20: it said the call depth is 0 after any error, but a host error that does not go through `PR_RunError` (VM-2.1, BUILTIN-3.2) leaves it; replaced by VM-19.6.
**Withdrawn** 2026-10-20: it gave VM-2.2 the effects of a runtime error, which resets the call depth, where VM-2.2 fails as VM-2.1 does, a host error that keeps it; replaced by VM-19.7.

An opcode that fails writes no global and no field. It may already have set the argument count (a failing call) or counted against `profile` (VM-3.4). A builtin that fails may have written before it failed (`builtins.md`).

After a runtime error the call depth is 0. After a host error that does not go through `PR_RunError`, `PR_ExecuteProgram: NULL function` (VM-2.1, VM-2.2) or a builtin's `error` or `objerror` (BUILTIN-3.2), it is still the depth at the error. Either way the local stack is not reset: the slots the aborted functions saved stay in use, are never restored and are never released, since nothing outside `pr_exec.c` touches `localstack_used`. The globals keep the values they had when the error happened, including the locals of the aborted functions.

The errors this spec adds where id's C is undefined (VM-1.4, VM-2.4, VM-3.3, VM-7.3, VM-11.4, VM-12.5, VM-14.3, VM-15.6) are runtime errors with the effects of VM-19.1, VM-19.2 and VM-19.6. id has no message for them, so the message is the implementation's. VM-2.2 is the host error of VM-2.1.
A WAD2 file starts with a 12-byte header: the four bytes `WAD2` (0x57 0x41 0x44 0x32), then `numlumps` and `infotableofs` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.

If the first four bytes are not exactly `WAD2`, loading fails with the error `Wad file <name> doesn't have WAD2 id` (fatal in id's engine). `wad.h` comments the field "should be WAD2 or 2DAW", but the code accepts only `WAD2`; `WAD3` and `2DAW` fail.
A file of fewer than 12 bytes fails to load. id's code reads the header from the loaded buffer without checking its length, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
The engine finds `gfx.wad` through the game filesystem (FS-3), so a mod can replace it; if it is not found, the engine stops with the fatal error `W_LoadWadFile: couldn't load gfx.wad`.

The directory is `numlumps` 32-byte entries at offset `infotableofs`: `filepos`, `disksize` and `size` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers, then the `type` and `compression` bytes, two unused bytes and a 16-byte name.
`numlumps` 0 gives an archive with no lumps, which loads without error.

A negative `numlumps` fails to load. id's loop compares an unsigned counter with it, so it walks about four billion entries past the buffer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

A directory that does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `infotableofs`, or `infotableofs + 32 * numlumps` past the end) fails to load. id's code does not check it, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

Each lump name is cleaned when the archive loads (`W_CleanupName`): the bytes of the 16-byte field up to the first NUL are kept, ASCII `A` to `Z` become `a` to `z`, every other byte (including 0x80 to 0xFF) is unchanged, and the rest of the field is filled with NUL. The comment above `W_CleanupName` says it pads with spaces; the code pads with NUL. Bytes after the first NUL are discarded.
A 16-byte name field with no NUL keeps all 16 bytes as the name. id's `strcmp` on such a name reads past the field, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as a 16-byte name.

`type`, `compression` and `disksize` are not checked. The engine uses `type` only to byte-swap the width and height of `TYP_QPIC` (66) lumps, which changes nothing on little-endian hosts. `compression` is ignored: `CMP_LZSS` (1) is defined in `wad.h` but no WinQuake code decompresses a lump, so a lump's bytes are always returned as stored.
`filepos`, `disksize` and `size` are not checked when the archive loads, so a bad range never stops an archive from loading or its directory from being listed.
Lumps keep their directory order, and two lumps may have the same cleaned name.

A lookup cleans the requested name by the rule of WAD-2.5 and returns the first lump, in directory order, whose cleaned name equals it. Lookups therefore ignore ASCII case (`CoNcHaRs` finds `CONCHARS`) but not the case of bytes 0x80 to 0xFF.

Only the first 16 bytes of the requested name count. A requested name of 16 or more bytes is compared as its first 16 bytes; id's code compares an unterminated buffer there, which is undefined, and this spec fixes the answer by WAD-2.6.
A name that matches no lump is the error `W_GetLumpinfo: <name> not found` (fatal in id's engine).

A lump's data starts at `filepos`. QuakeC Studio reads a lump as the `disksize` bytes at `filepos` (the bytes stored in the file; the engine itself never needs a length), and reading a lump whose range does not lie wholly inside the file is an error. The lump is still listed (WAD-2.8).

Looking up a lump by index accepts 0 to `numlumps - 1`. id's `W_GetLumpNum` accepts `numlumps` too (its test is `num > wad_numlumps`), which reads one entry past the directory; this spec fixes `numlumps` as an error. `W_GetLumpNum` has no caller in WinQuake (GitHub code search of `id-Software/Quake`, 2026-10-16, finds it only in `wad.c` and `wad.h`).
A picture lump (`TYP_QPIC`) is a `width` and a `height`, signed 32-bit little-endian, followed by `width * height` bytes of palette indices, row by row from the top left.

The `conchars` lump has no header: it is 128 by 128 bytes of palette indices, 16 rows of 16 characters of 8 by 8 pixels, character `n` at row `n >> 4` and column `n & 15`, with index 0 drawn as transparent.

A texture lump (`TYP_MIPTEX`) starts with a `miptex_t`: a 16-byte name, then `width`, `height` and four mip offsets as unsigned 32-bit little-endian integers, the offsets from the start of the lump. id's engine never reads a texture lump from a WAD; the same structure in a BSP file is the BSP spec's, and WAD2 texture files are read only by map tools and editors.

A chunk is a 4-byte id, a signed 32-bit little-endian length, and that many bytes of data. The next chunk starts `8 + ((length + 1) & ~1)` bytes after the chunk's start: the data is padded to an even length.

Finding a chunk walks the chunks from a start offset to the end of the file and returns the first whose id equals the four bytes asked for, compared exactly (case matters). The lengths of enclosing chunks, including the `RIFF` chunk's, are not used: every search runs to the end of the file.
A search stops, finding nothing, at a chunk whose length is negative, or when the next chunk would start at or past the end of the file.

A search also stops, finding nothing, when fewer than 8 bytes are left for a chunk header. id's code reads the header past the end of the buffer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as not found.

The next chunk's offset is computed without overflow: a length of 2147483647 puts the next chunk past the end of the file, so the search stops. In id's code `length + 1` overflows a signed integer there, which is undefined.

The file must contain a `RIFF` chunk, found by WAV-1 from the start of the file, whose bytes 8 to 11 are `WAVE`. Otherwise reading fails with the error `Missing RIFF/WAVE chunks`. The `RIFF` chunk need not be the first chunk in the file, and one that ends before byte 12 is missing.
Every later search starts 12 bytes after the start of the `RIFF` chunk.
A `fmt ` chunk must be found, or reading fails with the error `Missing fmt chunk`. Its format tag must be 1, or reading fails with the error `Microsoft PCM format only`.

`channels` is the signed 16-bit value at offset 10 of the `fmt ` chunk, `rate` the signed 32-bit value at 12 and `width` the signed 16-bit value at 22 divided by 8, with C integer division truncating toward zero (16 bits give 2, 12 give 1, 7 give 0). The `fmt ` chunk's own length is not checked: a short chunk's fields come from the bytes after it.
A `fmt ` field that lies past the end of the file fails reading with the error `Missing fmt chunk`. id's code reads past the buffer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

If a `cue ` chunk is found, `loopstart` is the signed 32-bit value at offset 32 of it, the sample offset of the first cue point; the number of cue points and the chunk's length are not checked. With no `cue ` chunk, `loopstart` is -1. A value past the end of the file is read as if there were no `cue ` chunk (id's code reads past the buffer, which is undefined).

After a `cue ` chunk, a `LIST` chunk is searched for from the chunk after the `cue ` chunk. If one is found and its bytes 28 to 31 are `mark`, the loop's sample count `samples = loopstart + n`, where `n` is the signed 32-bit value at offset 24. Bytes 28 to 31 past the end of the file mean no `mark`.

A `data` chunk must be found, or reading fails with the error `Missing data chunk`. id's code prints the message and returns what it has read, so the engine then plays the bytes at the start of the file as samples; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
`width` 0 fails reading with the error `Sound <name> has a bad sample width`. id's code divides the `data` length by it, which on x86 stops the program with a divide error.

The `data` chunk's sample count is its length divided by `width`, truncating toward zero, and `dataofs` is 8 bytes after the start of the chunk. When WAV-2.7 gave a non-zero `samples`, the data's count must be at least that, or reading fails with the error `Sound <name> has a bad loop length` (fatal in id's engine); otherwise `samples` is the data's count.

A loop length from WAV-2.7 that is negative, or whose sum overflows a signed 32-bit integer, fails reading with the error `Sound <name> has a bad loop length`. id's code overflows a signed integer, which is undefined, or keeps a negative length the mixer cannot play; this spec fixes both as an error.

The `data` chunk's length is not checked against the file. `samples` counts what the chunk declares; a reader gets only the sample bytes that lie inside the file, and the samples after them are silence. id's code reads past the buffer there, which is undefined.
A sound plays only if `channels` is 1. Any other value, including the 0 a failed `GetWavinfo` leaves, makes the engine print `<name> is a stereo sample` and not load the sound (not fatal).

A sample is 8-bit unsigned with 128 as silence when `width` is 1, and 16-bit signed little-endian when `width` is 2. Any other `width` fails with the error `<name> has a bad sample width`: `ResampleSfx` reads any width but 2 as 8-bit samples while keeping the width as given, so id's engine has no single meaning for it, and this spec fixes the answer as an error.

`rate` must be greater than 0, or loading fails with the error `<name> has a bad sample rate`. id's code divides the sample count by `rate` divided by the output rate and converts the result to an integer, which for 0 or less is undefined or a negative allocation; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
`loopstart` -1 means the sound does not loop; any other value is the sample the sound loops back to, and is not checked against `samples`.

`S_LoadSound` loads the sound named `<name>` (the name `precache_sound` and `sound` give) from the file `sound/<name>` only: `Q_strcpy(namebuffer, "sound/");` then `Q_strcat(namebuffer, s->name);`, and `COM_LoadStackFile(namebuffer, ...)`. A `.wav` file anywhere else on the search path is never loaded as a sound, so the checks of WAV-3.1 to WAV-3.4 say nothing about it. The 2021 rerelease ships such files, its DualSense haptics clips under `tactile/dualsense/` (stereo, which WAV-3.1 would reject), read only by its own engine.
